lessons.title: Lab: Hypersonic flow – Newtonian theory and stagnation heating

scenes.text: A capsule re-entering at several km/s compresses the air so violently that its shock layer glows.
Designers need pressure and temperature estimates for the heat shield.

steps.title: Hypersonic features (M > 5)
steps.body:
- **Thin shock layer**: the shock lies very close to the body.
- **Entropy layer** and **viscous interaction**.
- **High-temperature (real-gas) effects**: vibrational excitation, dissociation of O₂ (≥ ~2,500 K) and N₂ (≥ ~4,000 K), ionisation — the γ = 1.4 perfect-gas model fails.
- **Mach-number independence**: pressure and force coefficients become nearly independent of M∞.

**Newtonian theory**: particles hit the surface and lose their normal momentum: **Cp = 2 sin²θ_s** (θ_s = angle between the surface and the free-stream direction), a good estimate on the windward side; leeward Cp ≈ 0. **Cp,max** at the stagnation point is the Rayleigh pitot value: ≈ 1.83 at M = 10 (→ 1.84 as M → ∞); *modified Newtonian*: Cp = Cp,max sin²θ_s.

**Perfect-gas stagnation temperature**: T0 = T∞(1 + 0.2M∞²). Real flight temperature is lower because dissociation absorbs energy.

steps.title: Solved example: wedge
steps.body: A 10° half-angle wedge in hypersonic flow: Newtonian Cp = 2 sin²10° = **0.0603**. The exact oblique-shock value at M = 10 is ≈ 0.086: Newtonian theory under-predicts by about 30% for such a shallow wedge and is better for blunt, steeply inclined surfaces.

steps.title: Solved example: stagnation temperature at M = 10, 30 km
steps.body: T∞ = 226.5 K: T0 = 226.5×(1 + 0.2×100) = **4,756 K** (perfect gas). The actual temperature of the air at the stagnation point is far lower because dissociation absorbs energy: the perfect-gas value is an upper bound. Flight speed V = 10×301.7 = 3,017 m/s.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the perfect-gas T0 as the real temperature.
- Applying Newtonian theory to the leeward side (Cp ≈ 0 there).
- Using M independence below M ≈ 5.

steps.title: Visualisation methods
steps.body:
- **Schlieren**: shows density gradients (first derivative): knife-edge at the focus.
- **Shadowgraph**: second derivative of density; simple and cheap.
- **Interferometry**: density directly.
- **Oil-flow, PSP/TSP (pressure/temperature-sensitive paint)** for surface flow and loads.

Mach number from a **Mach wave** (weak disturbance, e.g. a scratch on the wall): **M = 1/sin μ**. Wedge shock check: use the θ–β–M relation.

steps.title: Solved example: Mach lines
steps.body:
A Mach line makes 25° with the stream: M = 1/sin25° = 1/0.4226 = **2.37**.
Wedge half-angle 10° with shock angle β = 39.3° gives M ≈ 2.0 by θ–β–M (consistent with the earlier example).

steps.body: Static pressure upstream 20 kPa, measured β = 39.3° at M = 2: M_n1 = 1.267 → p2/p1 = 1.706 → p2 = 34.1 kPa.

steps.title: Common mistakes

- Measuring the shock angle from the wedge surface rather than the flow direction.
- Using a strong shock's angle from a blurry edge.
- Treating the wall boundary-layer shock interactions as 2-D.

lessons.title: Formula and key-point sheet (γ = 1.4)

story.title: A single page before the exam

scenes.text: You are allowed to bring only your own memory: so you condense compressible flow into one page.
The page is organised by flow type.

steps.title: Shocks and expansions
steps.body:
- Normal: M2² = (1 + 0.2M1²)/(1.4M1² − 0.2); p2/p1 = 1 + 1.1667(M1² − 1); ρ2/ρ1 = 2.4M1²/(0.4M1² + 2); T0 constant; p0 falls.
- M1 = 2: M2 = 0.577, p2/p1 = 4.5, T2/T1 = 1.6875, p02/p01 = 0.721.
- Oblique: M_n1 = M1 sinβ; M2 = M_n2/sin(β − θ); tanθ = 2cotβ (M1²sin²β − 1)/(M1²(γ + cos2β) + 2).
- Prandtl–Meyer: ν(M) = √6 tan⁻¹√((M²−1)/6) − tan⁻¹√(M²−1); ν(2) = 26.38°; ν2 = ν1 + θ.
- Rayleigh pitot: p02/p1 = 5.64 at M = 2.

steps.title: Fanno, Rayleigh, linear theories
steps.body:
- Fanno: 4fL*/D (M = 0.5) = 1.069; T0 const; M → 1.
- Rayleigh: T0/T0* (M = 0.5) = 0.691; q = cp ΔT0.
- Prandtl–Glauert: Cp = Cp0/√(1 − M²).
- Korn: M_dd = κ/cosΛ − (t/c)/cos²Λ − CL/(10cos³Λ).
- Ackeret: cl = 4α/√(M²−1); cd = 4α²/√(M²−1) (flat plate); double wedge cd,w = 4τ²/√(M²−1).
- Sears–Haack: D/q = (9π/2)(S_max/l)²; Newtonian Cp = 2sin²θ.

steps.title: Top mistakes to avoid
steps.body:
- Using M1 instead of M_n1 in oblique shocks.
- Applying isentropic p0 relations across shocks.
- Taking the subsonic root of A/A* in the diverging section for supersonic flow.
- Mixing °C and K.

lessons.title: Lab: Wall-pressure distribution in a convergent–divergent nozzle

scenes.text: A small C–D nozzle has 10 wall pressure taps connected to a scanner; the tank pressure p0 = 300 kPa.
You compare p/p0 along the nozzle with the isentropic prediction.

steps.title: Aim, apparatus, procedure
steps.body:
**Aim**: to measure p/p0 along a C–D nozzle for several back pressures and to identify the flow regimes and the Mach number distribution.
**Apparatus**: compressed-air supply, settling chamber, C–D nozzle with wall taps, pressure transducers, thermocouple for T0.
**Procedure**: record atmospheric pressure; set p0; run with a back pressure above the first critical, then lower it; record p at all taps at each condition; note when the throat chokes (tap pressure p/p0 = 0.528).

steps.title: Observation table (design M_e = 2, A_e/A* = 1.6875, p0 = 300 kPa, design exit p = 38.3 kPa)
steps.body:
| Station | A/A* | Theory p/p0 | Measured p (kPa) | Measured p/p0 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| inlet | 1.34 (sub) | 0.843 | 252.5 | 0.842 |
| throat | 1.00 | 0.528 | 158.7 | 0.529 |
| div 1 | 1.34 (sup) | 0.2025 | 61.0 | 0.203 |
| exit | 1.6875 | 0.128 | 38.9 | 0.130 |

The agreement (±1%) confirms isentropic flow. M at the 'div 1' tap: p/p0 = 0.2025 → M = 1.70.

steps.title: Sources of error
steps.body: Wall boundary layer, tap burrs, leakage, unsteady blow-down p0 drift, temperature drift, finite resolution of the transducer.

lessons.title: Lab: Supersonic wedge flow – shock angle and pitot calibration

scenes.text: A new supersonic tunnel must be calibrated before a student project.
You use a pitot probe and a 10° wedge with schlieren.

steps.title: Aim and method
steps.body:
**Aim**: to determine the test-section Mach number using (a) the Rayleigh pitot formula and (b) the shock angle of a wedge, and to compare them with the nozzle area ratio.
**Procedure**: record p1 (static wall tap) and p02 (pitot, downstream of the bow shock); photograph a 10° wedge in schlieren and measure β.

steps.title: Observations
steps.body:
| Quantity | Reading | Result |
|---|---|---|
| p1 | 38.2 kPa | |
| p02 (pitot) | 215.4 kPa | p02/p1 = 5.64 → M = 2.00 |
| wedge β (measured) | 39.3° | θ = 10° → M ≈ 2.0 (θ–β–M) |
| Mach line from a wall scratch | 30° | M = 1/sin30° = 2.0 |

All three methods agree: **M = 2.0**. The nozzle area ratio gives M = 1.99.

steps.title: Worked reduction
steps.body: Pitot ratio: 215.4/38.2 = 5.639. Rayleigh formula at M = 2 gives 5.640. Wedge: M_n1 = 2.0 sin39.3° = 1.267; p2/p1 = 1.706 → a wall tap on the wedge should read 65.2 kPa (1.706×38.2).

steps.title: Sources of error
steps.body: Tunnel flow non-uniformity, probe misalignment, boundary-layer on the wedge, schlieren angle reading (±0.5°), transducer calibration.

lessons.title: Lab: Choked-flow nozzle for mass-flow measurement (with viva)

scenes.text: A 6 mm sonic nozzle is used as a calibrated flow meter: mass flow depends only on p0 and T0.
The viva examiner asks why back pressure does not matter.

steps.title: Aim and theory
steps.body:
**Aim**: verify ṁ = 0.0404 p0 A*/√T0 for choked flow and find the discharge coefficient C_d = ṁ_actual/ṁ_ideal.
**Apparatus**: critical-flow venturi nozzle, pressure transducer for p0, thermocouple for T0, and a reference flow meter.

steps.title: Observations and calculation
steps.body:
Throat d = 6 mm → A* = π(0.006)²/4 = 2.827×10⁻⁵ m². p0 = 600 kPa, T0 = 300 K: ṁ_ideal = 0.0404×600,000×2.827×10⁻⁵/√300 = **0.03957 kg/s**. Measured by reference: 0.0388 kg/s → C_d = 0.0388/0.03957 = **0.98**.

Back pressure: with p_b ≤ 0.528p0 = 317 kPa the reading is constant; at p_b = 400 kPa the nozzle unchokes and flow falls.

steps.title: Sources of error
steps.body: Boundary layer (C_d < 1), real-gas/humidity, thermocouple recovery factor, nozzle roughness.

activity.prompt: Typical viva questions with model answers.

items.q: Why does back pressure not change the mass flow once the nozzle is choked?
items.a: Information about downstream pressure cannot travel upstream through a sonic throat; the mass flux there is fixed by p0, T0 and A*.

items.q: What is the difference between stagnation and static pressure?
items.a: Stagnation pressure is the pressure if the flow were brought to rest isentropically; static pressure is what a moving fluid element feels.

items.q: What is an over-expanded nozzle?
items.a: One whose exit static pressure is below the ambient pressure; oblique shocks form at the exit.

items.q: Why does the shock cause loss in total pressure?
items.a: The shock is irreversible; entropy rises and p0 falls.

items.q: Why is T0 constant across a shock?
items.a: The flow is adiabatic with no work, so total enthalpy is conserved.

items.q: What is the use of a second throat in a supersonic tunnel?
items.a: It lets the starting shock be swallowed and keeps the test section supersonic while recovering pressure efficiently.

steps.title: Problem 2 – wedge (original)
steps.body:
Air at M = 3, p1 = 30 kPa, T1 = 220 K flows over a 20° wedge. Find p2, T2 and M2 (weak shock).
**Solution**: β = 37.76°; M_n1 = 1.837; p2/p1 = 3.77 → **p2 = 113 kPa**; T2/T1 = 1.559 → **T2 = 343 K**; M2 = 1.99.

steps.title: Problem 3 – expansion (original)
steps.body:
Flow at M = 2, p = 80 kPa expands round a 10° convex corner. Find M2 and p2.
**Solution**: ν1 = 26.38°; ν2 = 36.38° → M2 = 2.39; p2/p1 = 0.548 → **p2 = 43.8 kPa**.

steps.title: Problem 4 – nozzle (original)
steps.body:
A rocket-test nozzle has throat area 0.02 m², exit Mach 3, p0 = 2 MPa. Find A_e and p_e.
**Solution**: A/A* = 4.235 → A_e = 0.0847 m²; p0/p = 36.73 → **p_e = 54.5 kPa**.

lessons.title: Lab: ISA properties at 5,000 m

scenes.text: A turboprop is to operate from a hill airfield. The performance engineer must know how thin the air is at 5,000 m on a standard day.
She uses the ISA lapse-rate equations rather than a table lookup, so the spreadsheet works at any altitude.

steps.title: ISA troposphere (0–11 km)
steps.body:
Sea-level standard values: T0 = 288.15 K, p0 = 101,325 Pa, ρ0 = 1.225 kg/m³, lapse rate L = 0.0065 K/m.

- Temperature: **T = T0 − L·h**
- Pressure: **p = p0 (T/T0)^5.2559**
- Density: **ρ = ρ0 (T/T0)^4.2559**

The exponents come from hydrostatics dp = −ρ g dh with p = ρRT: g/(L R) = 9.80665/(0.0065×287.05) = 5.2559, and ρ exponent = 5.2559 − 1.

steps.title: Density altitude
steps.body: Aircraft respond to density, not altitude. On a hot day the *density altitude* is higher than the pressure altitude, so take-off runs lengthen and climb falls.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using °C instead of kelvin in the ratio T/T0.
- Using the pressure exponent (5.2559) for density.
- Applying the troposphere formula above 11 km (there T is constant at 216.65 K and p, ρ fall exponentially).

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **TAS** – true speed through the air.
- **EAS** – speed at sea level giving the same dynamic pressure: ½ρV² = ½ρ0·Ve², so **Ve = V√σ**, σ = ρ/ρ0.
- **Speed of sound** a = √(γRT), γ = 1.4, R = 287 J/kg·K.
- **Mach** M = V/a.

steps.title: Why EAS matters
steps.body: Aerodynamic loads and stall speed depend on dynamic pressure, so structural limits and stall are fixed in EAS (VEAS), while navigation uses TAS.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Dividing by √σ instead of multiplying when going TAS→EAS; and using a sea-level a (340.3 m/s) at altitude.

steps.title: Why cruise high
steps.body: Thinner air gives less drag for the same TAS, and jet engines run efficiently in cold air; the cold also lowers a, so a given TAS gives a higher Mach.

story.title: Sizing the engine of a trainer

scenes.text: A two-seat trainer of weight 10 kN, wing area 16 m², has CD0 = 0.03 and k = 0.05.
The powerplant engineer asks: how much power must the engine give at 50 m/s at sea level?

steps.title: Level-flight equations
steps.body:
Steady level flight: **L = W, T = D**. With q = ½ρV²:
- CL = W/(qS)
- CD = CD0 + k CL²
- D = q S CD, **power required Pr = D·V**.

Expanding: D = q S CD0 + k W²/(q S): parasite drag grows with V², induced drag falls with V², giving the classic U-shaped drag curve.

steps.title: Jet vs propeller
steps.body: A jet produces thrust, so thrust available is roughly constant with speed; a propeller aircraft produces power, so power available is roughly constant (propeller efficiency η, Pa = η·Pshaft).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Mixing power (W) and thrust (N), and using q in kPa with S in m² without converting.

lessons.title: Lab: Rate of climb from excess power

scenes.text: The trainer from the last lab must climb out over a ridge after take-off.
Its engine delivers 70 kW of useful propulsive power at 50 m/s.

steps.title: Climb equations
steps.body:
Resolving along the flight path in a steady climb at angle γ: T = D + W sinγ. Multiply by V: TV − DV = W V sinγ. Since V sinγ = h-dot (rate of climb):

**ROC = (Pa − Pr)/W** — excess power per unit weight.
Climb angle: sinγ = (T − D)/W.

steps.title: Best ROC vs best angle
steps.body: Best rate of climb (Vy) is at maximum excess power; best angle (Vx) is at maximum excess thrust, which is a lower speed. Obstacle clearance uses Vx.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Using ROC = Pa/W − D/W·V without keeping V; always subtract powers, not thrusts.

lessons.title: Lab: Gliding flight – angle, sink rate and distance

scenes.text: At 3,000 m the trainer's engine quits. The nearest airstrip is 35 km away.
Can she reach it in still air flying at best glide?

steps.title: Glide equations
steps.body:
With T = 0 and flight-path angle γ below horizon: L = W cosγ, D = W sinγ, so **tanγ = D/L = 1/(L/D)**. Sink rate = V sinγ. Range over ground = h × (L/D) (for small γ).
Best glide ratio = (L/D)max = 1/(2√(CD0 k)). Minimum sink needs minimum power required, a lower speed than best glide.

steps.title: Wind matters
steps.body: A 20 kt headwind cuts ground range; pilots add speed in a headwind (and slow down in sink) – the glide polar shifts. Real checklists allow safety margins.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Believing a heavier glider glides further (the ratio is unchanged; it just flies faster), and mixing best-glide and minimum-sink speeds.

lessons.title: Lab: Breguet range of a jet transport

scenes.text: A jet airliner cruises at 230 m/s with L/D = 17 and fuel burn c = 0.6 per hour (weight of fuel per unit thrust per hour).
It burns 20% of its take-off weight in cruise (W0/W1 = 1.25).

steps.title: Breguet equations (jet)
steps.body:
Fuel flow: −dW/dt = c T = c D = c W/(L/D). With V and L/D constant, integrating the range dR = V dt:

**R = (V/c)(L/D) ln(W0/W1)** and **endurance E = (1/c)(L/D) ln(W0/W1)**.
Propeller form: R = (η/c_p)(L/D) ln(W0/W1) with c_p weight of fuel per unit power per unit time. Here c must be in s⁻¹ (0.6 h⁻¹ = 1.667×10⁻⁴ s⁻¹).

steps.title: What drives range
steps.body: Range improves with V/c (efficient engine at high speed), aerodynamic efficiency L/D and structural efficiency (large W0/W1). For jets best range is at the speed where V/D is max, about 1.32 V_md.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Leaving c in per-hour while V is in m/s; and using the weight ratio the wrong way round (it is initial/final).

steps.title: Invert Breguet
steps.body: Solve for the weight ratio: **ln(W0/W1) = R c /(V L/D)**, so W1/W0 = exp(−R c/(V L/D)) and **fuel fraction = 1 − W1/W0**.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
R = 3×10⁶ m, c = 1.6667×10⁻⁴ s⁻¹, V = 230, L/D = 17.
R c = 500; V L/D = 3,910. ln ratio = 0.12788.
W1/W0 = e^−0.12788 = 0.8800 → fuel fraction **12.0%**.
For W0 = 700 kN that is 84 kN of fuel (about 10.7 tonnes).

steps.title: Real planning
steps.body: Operators add climb/descent allowances, alternate airport fuel, 5% contingency and final reserve (typically 30 min holding). The Breguet figure is the cruise core only.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Treating 12% as a weight in newtons; or forgetting the exponential (fuel burn per km falls as the aircraft lightens).

uni-aero-propulsion.description: Full B.Tech Aircraft Propulsion syllabus: thrust and efficiencies, ideal and real gas-turbine cycles, inlets, combustors and nozzles, axial and centrifugal turbomachinery, propellers, turboprops, ramjets and scramjets, and rocket propulsion, with solved numericals and laboratory practicals. courses.title: Unit 1 · Thrust, efficiencies and gas-turbine cycles
courses.summary: The thrust equation, propulsive/thermal/overall efficiency, TSFC, the ideal Brayton cycle, ideal turbojet cycle analysis station by station and the turbofan bypass benefit. Covers topics commonly taught in Indian B.Tech aerospace programmes.
outcomes: Apply the thrust equation to jet engines
Compute propulsive, thermal and overall efficiency and TSFC
Analyse the ideal Brayton cycle

lessons.title: Lab: The thrust equation

scenes.text: A jet engine takes in air, adds energy, and throws it out faster.
Newton's second law applied to a control volume gives the thrust.

steps.title: Control-volume derivation
steps.body:
Take a control volume around the engine in steady flow. Air mass flow ṁ_a enters at flight speed V₀; fuel ṁ_f is added (f = ṁ_f/ṁ_a); gas leaves at V_e with exit static pressure p_e over area A_e. Momentum balance along the axis:

**F = ṁ_a[(1 + f)V_e − V₀] + (p_e − p₀)A_e**

The first term is the momentum thrust (net of inlet momentum drag), the second the pressure thrust (zero for a fully expanded nozzle p_e = p₀). **Specific thrust** F/ṁ_a (N·s/kg). For a rocket there is no intake: F = ṁ V_e + (p_e − p₀)A_e. Uninstalled thrust excludes nacelle drag and installation losses (spillage, bleed, power extraction).

steps.title: Solved example: pressure thrust
steps.body: If the nozzle exit is under-expanded with p_e = 60 kPa, p₀ = 40 kPa, A_e = 0.30 m²: the pressure term = (60 − 40)×10³×0.30 = **6,000 N**, adding 6,000 N to the momentum thrust of 18,100 N for a total of 24,100 N.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the intake momentum ṁ_a V₀ ('ram drag').
- Using total (1+f) factor for fuel only when the fuel flow is non-negligible (it is ~2%).
- Mixing TSFC units (kg/(N·s), mg/(N·s), kg/(N·h)).

activity.prompt: ṁ_a = 50 kg/s, V₀ = 250 m/s, V_e = 600 m/s, f = 0.02, p_e = p₀. Net thrust in N.

lessons.title: Lab: Propulsive, thermal and overall efficiency

story.title: Why a slow big jet beats a fast small jet

scenes.text: A swan flaps a lot of air slowly; a firecracker blasts a little air quickly. The first is far more efficient at moving you.
Efficiency has two parts: turning fuel into kinetic energy, and turning that kinetic energy into thrust power.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Thermal efficiency η_th = (rate of increase of kinetic energy of the flow)/(rate of heat input)** = ½[(ṁ_a + ṁ_f)V_e² − ṁ_a V₀²]/(ṁ_f LHV).
- **Propulsive efficiency η_p = thrust power/(rate of KE increase) = F V₀/ΔKĖ**; for f ≈ 0 and p_e = p₀: **η_p = 2/(1 + V_e/V₀)**.
- **Overall efficiency η_o = η_th η_p = F V₀/(ṁ_f LHV)**. Also **TSFC = V₀/(η_o LHV)** — so at a given flight speed, lower TSFC means higher η_o.
- η_p is high when V_e ≈ V₀ (large mass flow, small velocity increase): the case for high-bypass turbofans and propellers; but η_p → 1 means F → 0 for the same ṁ.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the η_p = 2/(1 + V_e/V₀) approximation when fuel flow and pressure thrust matter.
- Forgetting that η_th depends on cycle pressure ratio and turbine inlet temperature, η_p on jet velocity.
- Comparing TSFC at different flight speeds.

activity.prompt: Propulsive efficiency η_p = 2/(1 + V_e/V₀) for V₀ = 250 m/s, V_e = 600 m/s (3 decimals).

quiz.q: TSFC = V₀/(η_o LHV) implies lower TSFC when

lessons.title: Lab: The ideal Brayton cycle

story.title: The cycle inside every gas turbine

scenes.text: Compress, heat at constant pressure, expand, reject heat: George Brayton's cycle is the model of every jet engine.
You compute efficiency and net work for a pressure ratio of 10.

steps.title: Ideal cycle
steps.body:
Processes: 1–2 isentropic compression; 2–3 heat addition at constant pressure; 3–4 isentropic expansion; 4–1 heat rejection at constant pressure. With r_p = p₂/p₁ and calorically perfect gas:

**η_th = 1 − 1/r_p^{(γ−1)/γ} = 1 − T₁/T₂** (independent of turbine inlet temperature).
**w_c = c_p(T₂ − T₁)**, **w_t = c_p(T₃ − T₄)**, **w_net = w_t − w_c**, specific work maximised for **T₂ = √(T₁T₃)** i.e. r_p,opt = (T₃/T₁)^{γ/(2(γ−1))}.
Real cycles lose through component efficiencies (η_c, η_t ≈ 0.85–0.92), pressure losses and cooling air; thermal efficiency of modern engines reaches about 0.40–0.55 (large turbofans, core-based).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the air-standard γ = 1.4 for the hot section (γ ≈ 1.33).
- Forgetting that higher r_p increases efficiency but lowers specific work beyond r_p,opt.
- Treating the Brayton cycle as having compressor work negligible: it is about 40% of turbine work.

lessons.title: Lab: Ideal turbojet cycle analysis

scenes.text: A fighter cruises at Mach 0.8 and 10 km altitude with a single-spool turbojet.
You will track T and p through stations 0 (ambient), 2 (compressor face), 3, 4, 5 and 9 (exit).

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
Ideal components: isentropic inlet, compressor and turbine; no pressure loss in the combustor; nozzle expands fully to p₀. Procedure:
1. Ambient conditions → V₀ = M₀a₀; T₀₂ = T₀(1 + 0.2M₀²); p₀₂ = p₀(1 + 0.2M₀²)^3.5.
2. Compressor: T₀₃ = T₀₂ π_c^{(γ−1)/γ}; p₀₃ = π_c p₀₂.
3. Combustor: T₀₄ given (limit); p₀₄ = p₀₃; fuel-air ratio f = c_p(T₀₄ − T₀₃)/LHV.
4. Turbine drives the compressor: T₀₅ = T₀₄ − (T₀₃ − T₀₂); p₀₅ = p₀₄(T₀₅/T₀₄)^{γ/(γ−1)}.
5. Nozzle: T₉ = T₀₅(p₀/p₀₅)^{(γ−1)/γ}; V₉ = √(2c_p(T₀₅ − T₉)).
6. Specific thrust F/ṁ = V₉ − V₀ (neglecting f); TSFC = f/(F/ṁ).

steps.title: Solved example: engine size
steps.body: For a required thrust F = 60 kN: ṁ_a = 60,000/853 = **70.3 kg/s**; fuel flow = 0.0212×70.3 = 1.49 kg/s.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using static T instead of stagnation T₀₂ for the compressor inlet.
- Forgetting the work balance (turbine work = compressor work).
- Taking p₀₅ = p₀₄.

activity.prompt: From the ideal turbojet analysis: nozzle exit velocity V₉ = √(2c_p(T₀₅ − T₉)) with T₀₅ = 1159.4 K and T₉ = 564.9 K (m/s).

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – Turbofan bypass benefit

scenes.text: On a modern airliner engine the fan moves five to ten times more air around the core than through it.
The result: more thrust from the same core and much lower fuel burn.

steps.title: Bypass ratio
steps.body: **Bypass ratio B = ṁ_bypass/ṁ_core**. For separate unmixed jets (fully expanded): **F = ṁ_c[(V_c − V₀)] + ṁ_b[(V_b − V₀)]** (neglect fuel). The core's available energy is shared among more air, so the average jet velocity falls, raising η_p and lowering TSFC, while thrust per unit core flow increases. Trade-offs: larger frontal area and nacelle drag, weight, fan-blade tip speed, and installation limits (ground clearance).

steps.title: Solved example: fuel saving
steps.body: With the same fuel flow (core unchanged, f = 0.021 → 1.05 kg/s), TSFC falls from 1.05/18,000 = 5.83×10⁻⁵ to 1.05/33,000 = **3.18×10⁻⁵ kg/(N·s)**, a 45% reduction.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the bypass ratio as a fraction of total flow.
- Ignoring fan pressure ratio when choosing V_b (V_b follows from the fan work).
- Forgetting that the extra thrust requires extra turbine work for the fan (so the core exit velocity V_c is lower than in the bare turbojet).

lessons.title: Lab: A real turbojet – component efficiencies and losses

scenes.text: A real engine has friction in the compressor, pressure loss in the combustor and mechanical losses in the shaft.
You redo the Mach 0.8 turbojet calculation with realistic component data.

steps.title: Component models
steps.body:
- **Inlet**: total pressure recovery π_d (0.95–0.99): p₀₂ = π_d p₀(1 + 0.2M₀²)^3.5.
- **Compressor**: isentropic efficiency η_c = (T₀₃s − T₀₂)/(T₀₃ − T₀₂) → **T₀₃ = T₀₂[1 + (π_c^{(γ−1)/γ} − 1)/η_c]**.
- **Combustor**: pressure ratio π_b (0.94–0.96), combustion efficiency η_b (0.98–0.995): f = c_p,b(T₀₄ − T₀₃)/(η_b LHV).
- **Turbine**: η_t, mechanical efficiency η_m: **η_m c_p,t(T₀₄ − T₀₅) = c_p,c(T₀₃ − T₀₂)(1 + bleed/mass-flow corrections)**; **T₀₅s = T₀₄ − (T₀₄ − T₀₅)/η_t**; p₀₅ = p₀₄(T₀₅s/T₀₄)^{γ_t/(γ_t−1)}.
- **Nozzle**: π_n (0.97–0.99), η_n: T₉ = T₀₅ − η_n(T₀₅ − T₉s).
Use cold section γ = 1.4, c_p = 1,005; hot section γ = 1.33, c_p = 1,148 J/kg·K.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using a single γ for the whole engine.
- Forgetting η_c in the compressor temperature rise.
- Applying the turbine pressure ratio formula with the actual rather than the isentropic temperature drop.

lessons.title: Lab: Parametric study – effect of compressor pressure ratio

scenes.text: Early jets had π_c ≈ 4–6; today's large engines exceed 40.
You compute the trend with the ideal cycle at M₀ = 0.8, T₀₄ = 1,500 K.

steps.title: Method
steps.body: Use the ideal turbojet procedure with different π_c and T₀₄ fixed. Quantities: τ_c = π_c^{0.2857}, T₀₃ = T₀₂τ_c, T₀₅ = T₀₄ − (T₀₃ − T₀₂), p₀₅/p₀₄ = (T₀₅/T₀₄)^{3.5}, V₉, F/ṁ, f, TSFC. Trends: specific thrust has a maximum at moderate π_c; TSFC falls with π_c (higher thermal efficiency); specific thrust rises with T₀₄ but TSFC also rises, and the turbine-material/cooling limit sets T₀₄.

steps.title: Solved example: effect of T₀₄
steps.body: At π_c = 20 raising T₀₄ from 1,500 to 1,700 K: T₀₅ = 1,359.4 K, V₉ rises to ≈ 1,202 m/s → F/ṁ ≈ 963 N·s/kg (+13%), but f rises to 0.0259 and TSFC to ≈ 2.69×10⁻⁵ (+8%). More thrust per kg air = smaller engine, but at the cost of fuel and turbine life.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming higher π_c always increases thrust.
- Ignoring that T₀₅ falls with π_c at fixed T₀₄ (less heat available for the jet).
- Forgetting practical limits: compressor exit temperature and blade materials.

lessons.title: Lab: Real separate-jet turbofan with fan work

story.title: Paying for the fan with the core

scenes.text: The same turbine that drove only the compressor must now also drive a big fan.
You rebuild the cycle with B = 5 and a fan pressure ratio of 1.6.

steps.title: Method
steps.body: Fan: T₀₁₃ = T₀₂[1 + (π_f^{0.2857} − 1)/η_f]. Fan work per kg of core air = B c_p(T₀₁₃ − T₀₂). The turbine must supply compressor + fan work: η_m c_p,t(T₀₄ − T₀₅) = c_p[(T₀₃ − T₀₂) + B(T₀₁₃ − T₀₂)]. Then the core and fan jets are expanded to p₀. **F/ṁ_c = (1 + f)V_c − V₀ + B(V_b − V₀)**.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
π_f = 1.6, η_f = 0.88: 1.6^{0.2857} = 1.1437 → T₀₁₃ = 251.7[1 + 0.1437/0.88] = 292.8 K (rise 41.1 K). With p₀₁₃ ≈ 1.6×39.09 = 62.5 kPa the fan jet (nozzle π_n = 0.98): **V_b ≈ 364 m/s** (adequate fully-expanded estimate).
Fan work = 5×1005×41.1 = 206.5 kJ/kg core; compressor work (real, from the previous lesson) = 393.5 kJ/kg. Total = 600 kJ/kg: 0.99×1148×(1500 − T₀₅) = 600,000 → **T₀₅ = 972 K**.
Core jet: T₀₅s = 913.3 K → p₀₅ = 742.7×(0.6089)^{4.03} = 100.6 kPa → V_c = **783 m/s**.
**F/ṁ_c = 1.0221×783 − 239.6 + 5×(364 − 239.6) = 560.5 + 622 = 1,182 N·s/kg core**; TSFC = 0.0221/1182 = **1.87×10⁻⁵ kg/(N·s)** versus 2.72×10⁻⁵ for the turbojet: 31% lower.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the fan work in the turbine work balance.
- Treating the fan stream's fuel flow as non-zero (it is zero).
- Ignoring that a fan with higher B needs a lower π_f for best performance.

lessons.title: Lab: Breguet range and why TSFC matters

scenes.text: An airline wants to fly Delhi to London non-stop (about 6,700 km) and compares engine options.
The Breguet equation links TSFC to range.

steps.title: Breguet range (jet aircraft)
steps.body: For cruise at constant altitude and CL: **R = (V/c)(L/D) ln(W₀/W₁)** with c = TSFC × g (weight-based specific fuel consumption, s⁻¹), V true airspeed, W₀ initial and W₁ final weight. Endurance E = (1/c)(L/D) ln(W₀/W₁). Range ∝ V/(TSFC) × L/D: higher η_o (lower TSFC at the same V) increases range directly. The figure V/c × L/D is sometimes called the range factor.

steps.title: Solved example: fuel required
steps.body: For a 5,000 km mission with the turbofan: ln(W₀/W₁) = R c/(V L/D) = 5×10⁶×1.834×10⁻⁴/(240×17) = 0.2248 → W₀/W₁ = 1.252; fuel fraction = 1 − 1/1.252 = **20.1%** of take-off weight (plus reserves).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using TSFC in kg/(N·h) with V in m/s.
- Forgetting reserves, climb and descent.
- Using Breguet for propeller aircraft: there R = (η_p/c_p)(L/D) ln(W₀/W₁), η_p the propeller efficiency.

activity.prompt: Breguet range with V = 240 m/s, L/D = 17, c = 1.834×10⁻⁴ s⁻¹, W₀/W₁ = 1.25 (km).

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – Size the engines for a 150-seat twin-jet

scenes.text: The airline wants a twin-engine narrow-body with a take-off weight of 700 kN.
You must estimate the cruise thrust, take-off thrust and cruise fuel flow.

steps.title: Sizing logic
steps.body:
1. Cruise thrust = drag = W/(L/D) (steady level flight; use mid-cruise weight ≈ 0.9 W₀).
2. Take-off thrust is sized by the one-engine-inoperative climb gradient and field length: total take-off T/W ≈ 0.28–0.32 for a twin.
3. Fuel flow = TSFC × thrust.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
W₀ = 700 kN; mid-cruise W = 0.9×700 = 630 kN; L/D = 17 → drag = **37.1 kN** → 18.5 kN per engine.
Take-off: T/W = 0.30 → total 210 kN → **105 kN per engine** (cruise thrust is only 18% of take-off thrust).
Cruise fuel flow per engine: 18,530×1.87×10⁻⁵ = **0.347 kg/s = 1,248 kg/h** per engine; 2,496 kg/h for both engines.

steps.title: Check with range
steps.body: Fuel fraction 20% of 700 kN → 140 kN = 14.3 t of fuel; at 2,496 kg/h the cruise endurance ≈ 5.7 h; at 240 m/s that is 4,900 km: consistent with the Breguet result (4,964 km).

steps.title: Common mistakes

- Sizing from cruise thrust alone (take-off and climb govern).
- Mixing kN and N.

lessons.title: Lab: Subsonic inlets and diffusers

story.title: The air has to arrive gently

scenes.text: The compressor wants a slow, uniform, high-pressure stream at its face, whatever the aircraft is doing.
The inlet duct is a diffuser: it slows the flow and converts kinetic energy to pressure.

steps.title: Diffuser performance
steps.body: For a diffuser with inlet area A₁ and exit area A₂ in low-speed flow: ideal pressure-recovery coefficient **C_p,ideal = 1 − 1/AR²** (AR = A₂/A₁), actual C_p = η_d C_p,ideal. Total-pressure recovery **π_d = p₀₂/p₀₀**; ram recovery **η_r**. Key limits: the equivalent cone angle ≈ 7° (total) to avoid separation; boundary-layer bleed, vortex generators, S-ducts (distortion), lip design (spillage, separation at high angle of attack), and buzz/unstart in supersonic intakes. For subsonic cruise, π_d ≈ 0.97–0.995; nacelle drag/spillage drag matters at part-throttle.

steps.title: Solved example: ram pressure rise
steps.body: Flight at M₀ = 0.8: ideal p₀₂/p₀ = 1.5243. With π_d = 0.97, the effective ratio = 1.4786 → compressor face pressure at 10 km = 26.44×1.4786 = **39.1 kPa**; the 3% loss reduces thrust by about 4–5%.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using a larger area ratio than the separation limit allows.
- Confusing static pressure rise with total pressure loss.
- Ignoring inlet distortion at high angle of attack or in cross-winds.

lessons.title: Lab: Supersonic intakes and pressure recovery

scenes.text: A fighter flying at Mach 2 must slow the air to M ≈ 0.4 for the compressor without losing too much total pressure.
Ramps, spikes and cones create several weak shocks instead of one strong one.

steps.title: Types
steps.body:
- **Pitot (normal-shock) intake**: simple, efficient to about M ≈ 1.6; recovery = normal-shock p₀₂/p₀₁.
- **External compression**: oblique shocks on a ramp or cone ahead of the cowl, then a normal shock; the lip is the 'shock-on-lip' design point.
- **Mixed compression**: part of the compression happens in the converging internal duct, ending with a terminal normal shock at the throat; good recovery above M ≈ 2.2 but needs a variable geometry and has unstart risk.
- **Internal compression**: all inside the duct; starting problems.
**Military specification recovery law (MIL-E-5008B)**: **η_r = 1 − 0.075 (M₀ − 1)^{1.35}** for 1 < M₀ < 5 (a design target for a good multi-shock intake).

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
M₀ = 2: MIL-spec η_r = 1 − 0.075×1 = **0.925** vs a normal-shock intake 0.721.
M₀ = 3: η_r = 1 − 0.075×2^{1.35} = 1 − 0.075×2.549 = **0.809** vs normal shock 0.328.
At M₀ = 2 and 11 km: p₀₀ = 177.1 kPa → compressor-face p₀₂ = 0.925×177.1 = **163.8 kPa** (vs 127.7 kPa for a pitot intake): a 28% gain.

steps.title: Solved example: mass flow capture
steps.body: If the freestream capture area A₀ is smaller than the cowl area A_c, the flow spills: spillage drag. Capture ratio A₀/A_c = 0.85 means 15% of the flow spills around the cowl (additive drag penalty).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the normal-shock recovery at M₀ > 2 in a design calculation.
- Ignoring unstart/buzz and the need for bleed and variable ramps.
- Forgetting that the engine face needs M ≈ 0.4–0.5 regardless of flight Mach number.

activity.prompt: MIL-E-5008B recovery at M₀ = 3: η_r = 1 − 0.075(M₀ − 1)^1.35 (3 decimals).

lessons.title: Lab: Combustor design and fuel flow

story.title: A fire that must never go out

scenes.text: Inside the combustor, air at 40 atm and 700 K meets kerosene, and the flame must be stable at idle, at take-off and in a rainstorm.
The designer must burn efficiently, keep the walls cool and limit pollutants.

steps.title: Zones and requirements
steps.body:
Annular, can and can-annular combustors share a three-zone logic: **primary zone** (φ ≈ 1 for flame stability, with a recirculation zone from swirlers), **intermediate zone** (burn-out of CO/soot), **dilution zone** (adds air to bring temperature down to the turbine limit and shape the pattern factor). About 25–30% of the air enters through the swirler/primary holes; the rest cools the liner and dilutes.
Key metrics: combustion efficiency η_b (≈ 0.99+ at cruise), pressure loss (4–6% of p₀₃), pattern factor, altitude relight, lean blowout margin, emissions (NOx rises with flame temperature; CO and unburned hydrocarbons dominate at idle; soot/smoke at high power); **equivalence ratio φ = f/f_st**, f_st ≈ 0.068 for kerosene.
**Fuel flow**: ṁ_f = ṁ_a c_p,b(T₀₄ − T₀₃)/(η_b LHV).

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: ṁ_a = 40 kg/s, T₀₃ = 700 K, T₀₄ = 1,500 K, c_p,b = 1,150 J/kg·K, η_b = 0.99, LHV = 43 MJ/kg: ṁ_f = 40×1150×800/(0.99×43×10⁶) = 36.8×10⁶/42.57×10⁶ = **0.865 kg/s** (f = 0.0216). Overall φ = 0.0216/0.068 = **0.32**: lean overall, because dilution air is added after the primary zone (which burns near φ ≈ 1).

steps.title: Solved example: liner pressure loss
steps.body: A pressure loss of 5% on p₀₃ = 800 kPa wastes 40 kPa: at turbine inlet p₀₄ = 760 kPa. Loss in the ideal ratio τ-calculation: reduces the turbine's expansion ratio and thrust by about 2–3%.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the overall equivalence ratio as the primary-zone ratio.
- Ignoring heat loss and liner cooling air in the energy balance.
- Forgetting that NOx increases with temperature while CO/UHC rise at low power.

activity.prompt: Fuel flow: ṁ_a = 40 kg/s, c_p,b = 1150, T₀₃ = 700 K, T₀₄ = 1500 K, η_b = 0.99, LHV = 43 MJ/kg (kg/s).

lessons.title: Lab: Exhaust nozzles – choking and thrust

story.title: A nozzle that is choked at take-off

scenes.text: At take-off power the turbine exit pressure is more than twice ambient: the convergent nozzle chokes and an under-expanded jet leaves it.
You compute the throat conditions and the pressure thrust.

steps.title: Convergent and convergent–divergent nozzles
steps.body: For a convergent nozzle with total conditions p₀₅, T₀₅ and ambient p₀: it **chokes** if p₀₅/p₀ > ((γ+1)/2)^{γ/(γ−1)} (= 1.89 for γ = 1.4; 1.85 for γ = 1.33). When choked: throat M = 1, T* = T₀₅·2/(γ+1), V* = √(γRT*), p* = p₀₅(2/(γ+1))^{γ/(γ−1)}, and the thrust includes **pressure thrust (p* − p₀)A***. A convergent–divergent nozzle expands further to p_e (ideal when p_e = p₀); used for high pressure ratio engines (supersonic fighters, afterburning): variable geometry adjusts A₈/A₉. Real nozzles have velocity coefficient C_v (≈ 0.97–0.99) and discharge coefficient C_d.

steps.title: Solved example: static test (V₀ = 0)
steps.body:
p₀₅ = 200 kPa, T₀₅ = 1,100 K, p₀ = 26.4 kPa, γ = 1.33, R = 287. p₀₅/p₀ = 7.6 > 1.85: **choked**. T* = 1100×2/2.33 = 944 K; V* = √(1.33×287×944) = **600 m/s**; p* = 200×0.5403 = **108.1 kPa**; ρ* = 108,100/(287×944) = 0.399 kg/m³ → ṁ/A = 239.5 kg/(s·m²).
Per m² of throat: momentum thrust = 239.5×600 = 143.7 kN; pressure thrust = (108.1 − 26.4)×1000 = 81.7 kN → **F/A* = 225.4 kN/m²**. 36% of the thrust is pressure thrust: a C–D nozzle would recover part of it.

steps.title: Solved example: ideal expansion
steps.body: Fully expanding the same flow to 26.4 kPa: V_e = √(2×1148×1100×[1 − (26.4/200)^{0.2481}]) = √(2.5256×10⁶×(1 − 0.6051)) = √0.9974×10⁶ = **999 m/s**; specific thrust 999 m/s vs the convergent nozzle's effective F/ṁ = 225.4×10³/239.5 = 941 m/s: +6%.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting pressure thrust for a choked nozzle.
- Assuming a C–D nozzle is always better (over-expansion at low pressure ratio causes flow separation and losses).
- Using the stagnation pressure ratio incorrectly: p₀₅/p₀, not p₅/p₀.

activity.prompt: Choked nozzle: V* = √(γRT*) with γ = 1.33, R = 287, T* = 944 K (m/s).

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – Afterburner thrust augmentation

scenes.text: A fighter pilot selects 'reheat' for take-off or a supersonic dash: fuel is sprayed into the jet pipe behind the turbine.
Thrust jumps, fuel consumption explodes.

steps.title: Principle
steps.body: The turbine exit gas still contains unburnt oxygen (the core runs lean). An **afterburner** (reheat) burns more fuel in the jet pipe at nearly constant pressure, raising T₀₆ to 1,800–2,200 K without turbine-temperature limits; the nozzle throat must open (variable A₈) to keep the engine matched. Ideal exhaust speed V₉ ∝ √T₀₆ (same pressure ratio). Thrust gain 40–70%; TSFC rises 2–3× (roughly 1.8–2.5 kg/(daN·h) with reheat vs 0.7–0.9 dry).

steps.title: Solved example: when to use it
steps.body: Take-off ground roll ∝ 1/thrust: +40% thrust shortens it by roughly 30%. For a 5-minute supersonic dash the extra fuel is 1.37 kg/s × 300 s = 412 kg, so reheat is used only briefly.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating reheat as efficient: its marginal TSFC is very high.
- Forgetting the variable nozzle (area must increase to avoid raising turbine back pressure).
- Ignoring flame stabiliser (V-gutter) drag and total-pressure loss in dry operation.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Axial and centrifugal compressors, turbines and matching
courses.summary: Euler turbomachinery equation, velocity triangles and stage loading of axial compressors and turbines, centrifugal compressor slip, compressor maps, stall and surge, corrected parameters and stage counting for a core compressor. Covers topics commonly taught in Indian B.Tech aerospace programmes.
outcomes: Draw and compute velocity triangles for an axial compressor stage
Apply de Haller and stage temperature rise limits
Compute work and expansion ratio for an axial turbine stage
Use slip factor for centrifugal compressors
Read a compressor map and compute surge margin and corrected parameters

lessons.title: Lab: Axial compressor stage – velocity triangles and work

scenes.text: Each rotor blade of a compressor is a small wing that turns the flow; the stator then converts swirl to pressure.
The Euler turbomachinery equation tells how much work a stage can do.

steps.title: Euler's equation and velocity triangles
steps.body:
Moment of momentum applied to a rotor: **w = U(c_θ2 − c_θ1)** (J/kg) for equal radii (axial machine), so **ΔT₀ = w/c_p**. Triangles: U blade speed; c absolute velocity; w (or V_r) relative velocity; c_a axial component (assumed constant); angles α (absolute) and β (relative) from the axial direction; c_θ = U − c_a tanβ.

**Stage pressure ratio** π_s = [1 + η_s ΔT₀/T₀₁]^{γ/(γ−1)}. **Degree of reaction** R = (c_a/2U)(tanβ₁ + tanβ₂) (fraction of static enthalpy rise in the rotor); R = 0.5 gives symmetric blading. **De Haller number** w₂/w₁ ≥ 0.72 limits diffusion and avoids blade stall. Typical stage ΔT₀ ≈ 25–40 K (π_s ≈ 1.2–1.5).

steps.title: Why not turn the flow more?
steps.body: With β₂ = 40°: w₂ = 150/cos40° = 195.8; de Haller = 0.58 < 0.72: the blades would stall. More turning gives more work but needs lower diffusion; designers raise U (higher tip speed) instead, limited by shock losses on the blade (relative Mach number ≈ 1.2–1.4 at the tip of transonic fans).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Measuring angles from the tangential direction instead of from the axis.
- Mixing c_θ definitions (sign) for rotor and stator.
- Using T₀₁ of the stage with the overall compressor inlet temperature.

activity.prompt: Axial compressor stage: U = 300 m/s, c_a = 150 m/s, β₂ = 52° (tan52° = 1.280). Stage temperature rise ΔT₀ = U(U − c_a tanβ₂)/c_p (K).

options: half of the rise in the rotor

lessons.title: Lab: Axial turbine stage

story.title: A turbine does in one stage what the compressor needs ten for

scenes.text: Expanding flow is far more stable than compressing flow: a single turbine stage can drop the temperature by 100–200 K.
You compute work, loading and expansion ratio for a high-pressure turbine stage.

steps.title: Stage analysis
steps.body:
The stator (nozzle) accelerates the flow and adds swirl α₂; the rotor removes the swirl. **Work per kg: w = U(c_θ2 + c_θ3)** (c_θ3 negative if the rotor exit swirl is opposite). For axial exit (c_θ3 = 0): **w = U c_a tanα₂**. Temperature drop ΔT₀ = w/c_p,t.
**Loading coefficient ψ = w/U²** (≈ 1.0–2.0 for HP turbines); **flow coefficient φ = c_a/U** (≈ 0.4–0.8); reaction R ≈ 0.4–0.5 for lightly loaded stages, 0 for impulse stages. Efficiency η_t ≈ 0.88–0.92; stage expansion ratio from ΔT₀ and η_t: p₀₁/p₀₃ = (T₀₁/T₀₃s)^{γ/(γ−1)}.
Blade cooling (film, internal, thermal barrier coatings) allows T₀₄ above the metal melting point.

steps.title: Solved example: stage count
steps.body: The compressor demands total w = 1005×391.5 = 393.5 kJ/kg (real). Each such stage gives 150.1 kJ/kg → 393.5/150.1 = 2.6: ≥ 3 turbine stages (or 2 high-loading stages) are needed for a single spool; the bigger the fan, the more LP-turbine stages (5–7).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to use hot-gas c_p (≈ 1,148) in the turbine.
- Confusing the absolute swirl angle α₂ with the relative angle.
- Assuming ψ can be arbitrarily large: blade loading and stator Mach number limit it.

activity.prompt: Turbine stage: U = 350 m/s, c_a = 200 m/s, α₂ = 65°, axial exit. Work per kg w = U c_a tanα₂ (kJ/kg).

lessons.title: Lab: Centrifugal compressors – slip and pressure ratio

story.title: The compressor of a helicopter engine

scenes.text: Small turboshaft engines such as those on helicopters often use a centrifugal compressor stage for its high pressure ratio per stage and robustness.
You compute the pressure ratio from the tip speed.

steps.title: Impeller work and slip
steps.body: Air enters axially near the eye (c_θ1 ≈ 0) and leaves the impeller tip at radius r₂ with tangential velocity c_θ2 = σ U₂ (slip factor σ < 1 because the flow lags the blade): **w = σ U₂²** (+ power input factor ψ ≈ 1.04 for disc friction). **Stanitz slip factor σ = 1 − 0.63π/Z** (Z = number of blades), Wiesner σ = 1 − √(cosβ₂′)/Z^{0.7}. Pressure ratio: π_c = [1 + η_c σU₂²/(c_p T₀₁)]^{γ/(γ−1)}. Typical single-stage π_c = 4–8 with tip speeds 400–550 m/s; limited by tip Mach number and material stresses (U₂ ≲ 550 m/s for titanium impellers). Components: inducer, impeller, vaneless space, diffuser (vaned), scroll/crossover. Compared with axial: low efficiency (0.78–0.85) but wide flow range, short length, high pressure per stage, lower FOD sensitivity.

steps.title: Solved example: higher tip speed
steps.body: U₂ = 520 m/s: w = 0.896×520² = 242.3 kJ/kg → ΔT₀ = 241 K → π_c = (1 + 0.8×241/288)^{3.5} = (1.669)^{3.5} = **6.0**. The pressure ratio rises with U₂² (a 15.6% increase of U₂ gives 34% more work).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using σ = 1 (ideal) for the exit swirl.
- Neglecting inlet pre-whirl when present.
- Forgetting that increasing U₂ is limited by tip Mach number and stress.

activity.prompt: Centrifugal compressor: σ = 0.896, U₂ = 450 m/s, c_p = 1005, η_c = 0.80, T₀₁ = 288 K. Pressure ratio.

lessons.title: Lab: Compressor maps, stall, surge and corrected parameters

story.title: The bang of a compressor stall

scenes.text: Pilots remember the thump and flames from the engine when a compressor surges.
A compressor map shows where it can operate and where it cannot.

steps.title: Maps and parameters
steps.body:
Dimensional analysis: performance depends on **corrected speed N/√θ** and **corrected flow ṁ√θ/δ**, with θ = T₀₂/288.15 K and δ = p₀₂/101.325 kPa. The **compressor map** plots pressure ratio against corrected flow for lines of constant corrected speed and efficiency islands; the **surge line** bounds stable operation; the **operating (running) line** is set by the turbine nozzle area and matches the engine.
- **Rotating stall**: local blade-row stall cells that rotate at ≈ 50% of rotor speed.
- **Surge**: whole-system axial flow oscillation (violent).
- **Surge margin** = (π_surge − π_op)/π_op at constant corrected flow (or at constant speed); typically 15–25%.
Causes: inlet distortion, rapid throttle changes, damaged blades, hot gas ingestion. Remedies: bleed valves, variable inlet guide vanes/stators, multi-spool engines.

steps.title: Solved example: corrected parameters
steps.body:
At M₀ = 0.8, 10 km: T₀₂ = 251.7 K, p₀₂ = 40.30 kPa: θ = 0.8735, δ = 0.3977. If ṁ = 80 kg/s and N = 10,000 rpm: corrected flow = 80×√0.8735/0.3977 = 80×0.9346/0.3977 = **188.0 kg/s**; corrected speed = 10,000/0.9346 = **10,700 rpm**.
The same engine on a sea-level test stand at ISA (θ = 1, δ = 1) at 10,700 rpm passes 188 kg/s: test-cell results are scaled to flight conditions.

steps.title: Solved example: surge margin
steps.body: At a given corrected flow: surge-line pressure ratio 9.5, operating-line 8.0: SM = (9.5 − 8.0)/8.0 = **18.75%**. During a rapid throttle burst the operating line moves up toward the surge line (fuel flow rises faster than the spool): the control system schedules fuel acceleration limits and variable stator vanes to protect the margin.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using static rather than total conditions in corrected parameters.
- Confusing rotating stall (partial, steady) with surge (system-wide, oscillatory).
- Believing a higher pressure ratio always means better performance regardless of surge margin.

activity.prompt: Surge margin (percent) = (π_surge − π_op)/π_op with π_surge = 9.5 and π_op = 8.0.

options: flow oscillating through the whole machine
moving the operating point away from surge

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – Stage count for a 20:1 core compressor

scenes.text: The chief engineer wants a 20:1 compressor in a short engine.
You compute the number of axial stages from the stage temperature rise.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
1. Overall ΔT₀ from π_c and η_c: ΔT₀ = T₀₂(π_c^{(γ−1)/γ} − 1)/η_c.
2. Choose the stage ΔT₀ (limited by de Haller and tip speed).
3. Stages N = ΔT₀,overall/ΔT₀,stage (round up).
Stage pressure ratio decreases along the compressor because T₀₁ increases.

steps.title: Solved example: split into two spools
steps.body: Two spools with the LP compressor π = 4.5 and the HP compressor π = 4.4 (overall 19.8): each spool runs at its own speed: fewer stages (about 4 + 6 = 10, the LP spool carries the fan too). The multi-spool arrangement improves surge margin and starting, at the cost of mechanical complexity.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the front-stage π_s for all stages.
- Not rounding up the stage count.
- Forgetting that the real compressor needs variable stators at low speed to avoid front-stage stall.

activity.prompt: Number of stages N = ΔT₀,overall/ΔT₀,stage with 391.5 K overall and 32.2 K per stage (1 decimal).

lessons.title: Lab: Momentum (actuator-disc) theory of the propeller

story.title: Why a big slow propeller is efficient

scenes.text: A glider's tow-plane and a transport turboprop both use big, slowly turning propellers for the same reason a helicopter has a large rotor.
Rankine and Froude showed that efficiency improves when you accelerate a lot of air a little.

steps.title: Actuator disc
steps.body: Model the propeller as a disc of area A = πD²/4 that adds a pressure jump to the air. Far upstream V₀; at the disc V₀ + v_i; far downstream V_e = V₀ + 2v_i (the **Froude theorem**: half of the velocity increase occurs ahead of the disc). Thrust **T = ṁ(V_e − V₀) = ρA(V₀ + v_i)·2v_i**. Eliminating v_i: **V_e = V₀√(1 + T/(½ρA V₀²))**, ideal efficiency **η_i = T V₀/(T(V₀ + v_i)) = V₀/(V₀ + v_i) = 2/(1 + V_e/V₀)**. For static thrust (V₀ = 0): T = 2ρA v_i²; ideal power P = T v_i = T^{3/2}/√(2ρA). Real propellers: η_p = η_i × profile efficiency (≈ 0.85–0.9) and also lose swirl and tip losses.

steps.title: Solved example: why big diameter
steps.body: Same T and V₀ with D = 1.5 m (A = 1.767 m²): ratio = 3000/(0.6125×1.767×3600) = 0.770; V_e = 60√1.770 = 79.8; η_i = 120/139.8 = **0.858**: the smaller disc is 5% less efficient, so the larger propeller wins (until tip speed limits it).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the disc-loading formula at V₀ = 0 without the static formula.
- Confusing induced velocity v_i at the disc with the slipstream increment.
- Expecting η_i > 1 or ignoring the ideal limit.

lessons.title: Lab: Propeller coefficients, advance ratio and performance

scenes.text: A propeller manufacturer's chart gives thrust and power coefficients versus advance ratio.
You compute thrust, power and efficiency for a cruise condition.

steps.title: Non-dimensional coefficients
steps.body: With n (rev/s), D (m): **J = V₀/(nD)** (advance ratio), **C_T = T/(ρ n² D⁴)**, **C_P = P/(ρ n³ D⁵)**, **η = J C_T/C_P**. Tip speed **V_tip = π n D**; helical tip Mach M_h = √(V_tip² + V₀²)/a ≲ 0.85–0.9 to avoid compressibility losses. Blade pitch (fixed, ground-adjustable, variable, constant-speed) matches blade angle to J: **constant-speed propellers** adjust pitch so that the engine runs at its optimum rpm while η stays near its maximum over a range of J. Blade element theory integrates section lift and drag along the radius: dT = ½ρ W² c(C_l cosφ − C_d sinφ) dr, dQ similarly; combined with momentum theory it gives accurate predictions. Propellers also have static thrust (J = 0) very high, thrust falling with speed — hence propellers for low speed, jets for high speed.

steps.title: Solved example: thrust variation
steps.body: Because T ∝ n²D⁴ at fixed J-curve points, doubling rpm at the same J gives 4× thrust and 8× power. At constant power, thrust falls with speed: T = ηP/V₀: 159.2×0.674/60 = 1,788 N at 60 m/s, but only ≈ 1,100 N at 100 m/s if η stays 0.69 (T = 0.69×159,200/100 = 1,098 N).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using rpm instead of rev/s in J, C_T and C_P.
- Forgetting D⁴/D⁵ scaling when changing size.
- Ignoring tip Mach number limits (noise and efficiency).

activity.prompt: Propeller efficiency η = J C_T/C_P with J = 0.789, C_T = 0.070, C_P = 0.082 (3 decimals).

lessons.title: Lab: Turboprops and turboshafts – power and thrust

scenes.text: On sectors under 800 km, a turboprop uses 20–30% less fuel than a similar regional jet.
A gas turbine drives the propeller through a reduction gearbox.

steps.title: Turboprop cycle
steps.body:
A turboprop is a gas generator plus a **free (power) turbine** driving a propeller via a reduction gearbox (propeller 1,000–2,000 rpm, turbine 10,000+ rpm). Nearly all the available energy is extracted as shaft power; a small residual jet thrust remains. 
**Total thrust: T = η_p P_sh/V₀ + F_jet.** **Equivalent shaft power (ESHP) = P_sh + F_jet V₀/η_p** (or the conversion about 1 hp per 2.5 lbf for static thrust). Specific fuel: **SFC = ṁ_f/P_sh** (kg/(kW·h): modern ≈ 0.25–0.30). Turboshafts power helicopters: **no jet thrust** (all energy to shaft; SFC 0.30–0.40 kg/kW·h).
High-speed limits: propeller efficiency falls above M ≈ 0.7 as tip Mach rises; advanced propellers (propfans, counter-rotating, scimitar blades) extend this.

steps.title: Solved example: comparison with a turbojet
steps.body: A turbojet of the same fuel flow (280 kg/h = 0.0778 kg/s) at TSFC = 5×10⁻⁵ kg/(N·s) produces 1,556 N at V₀ = 100 m/s; the turboprop gives 9,000 N, i.e. 5.8 times more thrust at low speed. At 250 m/s (M 0.75) the turboprop thrust falls to ≈ 0.85×1,000,000/250 = 3,400 N (with a lower η_p) while the jet's thrust is nearly unchanged: crossover near M = 0.6–0.7.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding propeller power and jet thrust directly (units differ): convert using η_p.
- Using static thrust-to-power ratios at cruise speeds.
- Ignoring gearbox and propeller-drive losses (≈ 2%).

lessons.title: Lab: The ideal ramjet

story.title: An engine with no moving parts

scenes.text: At Mach 2–3, shock compression alone gives a pressure ratio of 7–37, so you can drop the compressor and turbine.
The ramjet is a duct: intake, combustor, nozzle.

steps.title: Ideal ramjet cycle
steps.body: Ram compression gives T₀₂ = T₀₁ = T₀(1 + 0.2M₀²), p₀₂ = p₀(1 + 0.2M₀²)^3.5 (ideal). Heat addition to T₀₄ (limited by materials/dissociation) with p₀₄ = p₀₂. Nozzle expands to p₀: T₉ = T₀₄/(1 + 0.2M₀²) (since p₀₄/p₀ = (1+0.2M₀²)^{3.5}); V₉ = √(2c_p(T₀₄ − T₉)). **F/ṁ = V₉ − V₀**; fuel f = c_p(T₀₄ − T₀₂)/LHV. A ramjet has **zero static thrust** (needs a booster or launch speed M ≳ 0.5–1) and works best M 2–4; above M ≈ 5 the slowing of the whole flow to subsonic loses too much (shock loss and dissociation) → **scramjet**. Uses: missiles (e.g. air-launched anti-ship missiles), target drones, and some designs with turbine-based combined cycles.

steps.title: Solved example: M₀ = 3
steps.body: T₀ = 216.65 K, V₀ = 3×295.1 = 885 m/s. T₀₂ = 606.6 K. T₀₄ = 2,200 K: T₉ = 2200/2.8 = 785.7 K; V₉ = √(2×1005×1414.3) = **1,686 m/s**; F/ṁ = **801 N·s/kg**; f = 1.005×(2200 − 607)/43 = 0.0372; TSFC = 4.6×10⁻⁵. At M = 3 the ramjet is far more efficient than any turbojet (whose compressor would face T₀₂ ≈ 607 K).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Expecting thrust at zero airspeed.
- Using the ideal intake recovery at high Mach (real ramjet η_r ≈ 0.6–0.9 and significant combustor loss).
- Ignoring that the combustor inlet must be subsonic (≈ M 0.2–0.3).

activity.prompt: Ideal ramjet at M₀ = 2: V₉ = √(2c_p(T₀₄ − T₉)), T₀₄ = 2000 K, T₉ = 1111 K (m/s).

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – Which engine for which Mach number? (incl. scramjets)

scenes.text: A design team compares options for aircraft that cruise at M 0.5, 0.8, 2.5 and 6.
Indian programmes include ISRO's scramjet engine test (2016) and DRDO's hypersonic technology demonstrator flight (2020).

steps.title: Operating envelopes (typical)
steps.body:
- **Propeller/turboprop**: M ≲ 0.7, best below M 0.6.
- **High-bypass turbofan**: M 0.7–0.9 (airliners).
- **Low-bypass/afterburning turbofan or turbojet**: M 0.9–3.
- **Ramjet**: M 2–4 (needs boost to start).
- **Scramjet**: M ≳ 5–6 up to about 10–12; air passes through the engine at supersonic speed and fuel (typically hydrogen or endothermic hydrocarbon) is burned in a supersonic stream; mixing and ignition occur in milliseconds (flow residence ≈ 1 ms), so strut/cavity flame holders and pilot injection are used.
- **Rockets**: any Mach and altitude, but with low Isp.
Examples: NASA's X-43A reached about Mach 9.6 in 2004 (a few seconds of powered flight); ISRO tested a scramjet engine on its ATV-D02 sounding rocket in August 2016 (about 5 s at Mach ≈ 6); DRDO flew its Hypersonic Technology Demonstrator Vehicle in September 2020 (scramjet burn of about 20 s at Mach 6). Scramjet challenges: thermal protection, intake starting, short combustion time, drag losses, and control.

steps.title: Solved example: scramjet stagnation heating
steps.body: At M₀ = 6, T₀ = 217 K: T₀₂ = 217×(1 + 0.2×36) = 217×8.2 = **1,779 K** (perfect gas; actual lower due to dissociation). A diffuser that brought the flow to subsonic speeds would produce this temperature and heavy dissociation losses; a scramjet decelerates only to M ≈ 2–3 (T ≈ 700–1,000 K) and keeps the flow supersonic.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying scramjets work at all speeds: they need a rocket or turbine-based booster to ≥ Mach 4–5.
- Quoting only duration: flight-test data are brief (seconds), far from an operational engine.
- Ignoring thermal limits.

courses.title: Unit 6 · Rocket propulsion
courses.summary: Rocket thrust and specific impulse, the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation, nozzle theory with characteristic velocity and thrust coefficient, solid and liquid propellants, and staging with a launch-to-orbit capstone. Covers topics commonly taught in Indian B.Tech aerospace programmes.
outcomes: Compute thrust, effective exhaust velocity and I_sp
Apply the rocket equation and mass-ratio staging
Size a rocket nozzle using c* and C_F
Describe solid and liquid propellants and compute solid burn rate effects

lessons.title: Lab: Rocket thrust, effective exhaust velocity and specific impulse

story.title: Thrust in a vacuum is bigger

scenes.text: The same rocket engine produces more thrust and a higher specific impulse in space than at sea level.
The reason is the pressure term in the thrust equation.

steps.title: Thrust equation
steps.body: **F = ṁ V_e + (p_e − p_a) A_e.** Define the **effective exhaust velocity c = F/ṁ = V_e + (p_e − p_a)A_e/ṁ**, and the **specific impulse I_sp = F/(ṁ g₀) = c/g₀** (seconds, g₀ = 9.80665 m/s²). Total impulse I_t = ∫F dt. In vacuum p_a = 0 so F_vac = ṁV_e + p_e A_e. **Optimum (matched) expansion**: p_e = p_a → maximum thrust for a given chamber condition (a nozzle expanding to a lower p_e than p_a is over-expanded: separation risk). Typical vacuum I_sp: solid (APCP) 250–290 s; kerosene/LOX 330–350 s; LH₂/LOX 440–460 s; storable hypergolic (N₂O₄/UDMH) 310–330 s; hydrazine monopropellant 220 s; ion thrusters 2,000–5,000+ s.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
ṁ = 100 kg/s, V_e = 2,800 m/s, p_e = 60 kPa, A_e = 0.5 m², p_a = 101.3 kPa (sea level).
F = 100×2800 + (60 − 101.3)×10³×0.5 = 280,000 − 20,650 = **259,350 N**; I_sp(sea level) = 259,350/(100×9.80665) = **264.5 s**.
In vacuum: F_vac = 280,000 + 60,000×0.5 = **310,000 N**; I_sp,vac = **316.1 s**. The ratio 310/259 = 1.20: that is why upper stages have large expansion ratios while first stages use compromise nozzles.

steps.title: Solved example: burn time and impulse
steps.body: Propellant 20,000 kg at ṁ = 100 kg/s → burn time **200 s**. Total impulse (average F 290 kN) = 58 MN·s.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using I_sp in seconds with g = 9.81 incorrectly when comparing with c in m/s.
- Forgetting that the sea-level thrust is lower than the vacuum thrust.
- Quoting I_sp without specifying sea level or vacuum.

activity.prompt: Sea-level thrust: ṁ = 100 kg/s, V_e = 2800 m/s, p_e = 60 kPa, p_a = 101.3 kPa, A_e = 0.5 m² (N).

quiz.q: Vacuum thrust exceeds sea-level thrust by

lessons.title: Lab: The Tsiolkovsky rocket equation

scenes.text: A rocket carries its own reaction mass; the more it carries, the more it must accelerate.
The result is an exponential: velocity gain grows only with the logarithm of the mass ratio.

steps.title: Derivation and consequences
steps.body: Without gravity or drag: m dV = −c dm (momentum). Integrating from initial mass m₀ to final mass m_f: **Δv = c ln(m₀/m_f) = I_sp g₀ ln(m₀/m_f)**. With gravity (vertical ascent): Δv_net = Δv − g t_b; real launches lose ≈ 1.2–1.8 km/s to gravity, drag and steering. Mass ratio r = m₀/m_f = exp(Δv/c). **Propellant fraction ζ = 1 − 1/r**. **Structural coefficient ε = m_s/(m_s + m_p)**. For stage with payload fraction π_u = m_pl/(m_s + m_p): **r = (1 + π_u)/(ε + π_u)**.

steps.title: Solved example: Δv
steps.body: I_sp = 300 s, r = 5: Δv = 300×9.80665×ln5 = 2,942×1.609 = **4,735 m/s**. For Δv = 9,400 m/s (LEO with losses) with I_sp = 350 s (c = 3,432 m/s): r = e^{9400/3432} = e^{2.739} = **15.5** → 93.5% of the lift-off mass would have to be propellant: a single stage is impractical with ε ≈ 0.1.

steps.title: Solved example: a stage
steps.body: ε = 0.10, π_u = 0.20: r = 1.20/0.30 = **4.0**; Δv (I_sp = 300 s) = 2,942×ln4 = **4,078 m/s**. Two identical stages: Δv = 8,157 m/s with a payload of about 2.8% of lift-off mass (π_u = 0.2 for each stage).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using I_sp in seconds directly in the rocket equation (multiply by g₀).
- Forgetting that the rocket equation gives Δv in free space: add gravity, drag and steering losses.
- Mass ratio counted with payload incorrectly.

activity.prompt: Δv = I_sp g₀ ln(m₀/m_f) with I_sp = 300 s, m₀/m_f = 5 (m/s).

quiz.q: Doubling the mass ratio adds Δv of

lessons.title: Lab: Rocket nozzle theory – exhaust velocity, c* and C_F

scenes.text: A propulsion team must size the throat of a 100 kN engine running at 6.8 MPa chamber pressure.
They use the isentropic nozzle relations with chamber temperature and molecular weight.

steps.title: Ideal nozzle relations
steps.body: **V_e = √{ (2γ/(γ−1)) R T_c [1 − (p_e/p_c)^{(γ−1)/γ}] }**, R = R_u/M_w. **Characteristic velocity c\* = p_c A_t/ṁ = √(γ R T_c)/Γ(γ)** with Γ = √γ (2/(γ+1))^{(γ+1)/(2(γ−1))}. **Thrust coefficient C_F = F/(p_c A_t)** (ideal: C_F = V_e/c\* at p_e = p_a). Then **ṁ = p_c A_t/c\***, **F = C_F p_c A_t**, **I_sp = c\* C_F/g₀**. Higher T_c and lower M_w give higher V_e (hence LH₂/LOX); higher p_c and larger expansion ratio give higher C_F. Real values include nozzle efficiency (0.95–0.98) and combustion efficiency c\* (0.95–0.99).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using R = 287 J/kg·K (air) for rocket exhaust.
- Using chamber-state γ for the whole expansion (γ varies; shifting equilibrium).
- Forgetting c\* is a property of propellant/combustor, independent of the nozzle.

activity.prompt: Throat diameter for F = 100 kN: A_t = ṁ c*/p_c with ṁ = 35.3 kg/s, c* = 1773 m/s, p_c = 6.8 MPa. A_t in cm².

lessons.title: Lab: Chemical propellants – solid and liquid rockets

scenes.text: A solid motor is a pre-mixed fuel-oxidiser grain: simple, storable, impossible to shut down.
A liquid engine pumps fuel and oxidiser separately: complex, controllable, higher I_sp.

steps.title: Types
steps.body:
**Solid propellants**: composite (ammonium perchlorate oxidiser + aluminium powder + HTPB binder) with I_sp,vac ≈ 260–290 s, density ≈ 1,750 kg/m³; grain shapes (end burner, internal star/tube, finocyl) define thrust–time curves. **Burn rate (Vieille's law)**: **r = a p_c^n** (n < 1 for stable burning; n ≈ 0.2–0.5). Mass flow ṁ = ρ_p A_b r. Equilibrium chamber pressure p_c = [ρ_p a c\* (A_b/A_t)]^{1/(1−n)}.
**Liquid propellants**: LOX/RP-1 (kerosene) (I_sp,vac ≈ 330–350 s), LOX/LH₂ (≈ 430–460 s), storable hypergolics N₂O₄/UDMH (self-igniting, ≈ 310–330 s). Feed systems: pressure-fed or pump-fed (turbopump with gas generator, staged combustion or expander cycle); cooling: regenerative (the fuel cools the nozzle); injectors atomise and mix. India's PSLV first stage uses a large HTPB solid motor with liquid second stage (Vikas engine, N₂O₄/UH25); GSLV Mk III uses a cryogenic upper stage (LOX/LH₂).

steps.title: Solved example: pressure stability
steps.body: If cracks double A_b, equilibrium pressure rises by 2^{1/(1−n)} = 2^{1.538} = **2.9×** (chamber pressure triples): this is why grain cracks cause motor burst failures; n < 1 ensures a stable equilibrium.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Taking n ≥ 1 (unstable, can blow up).
- Mixing units of a (mm/s per MPa^n).
- Ignoring erosive burning and grain defects.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – Is this two-stage design enough for orbit?

story.title: The design review at ISRO-like scale

scenes.text: A small-satellite launcher team proposes two stages. Reviewers ask: does the Δv close?
You compute Δv and compare it with orbital speed plus losses.

steps.title: Orbit requirement
steps.body: Circular orbit speed **v_c = √(μ/r)** (μ = 3.986×10¹⁴ m³/s²; r = 6,378 km + altitude). Launch Δv budget: v_c + gravity/drag/steering losses (1.2–1.8 km/s) − Earth-rotation benefit (up to 0.46 km/s at the equator; for launch from Sriharikota at 13.7° N ≈ 0.45 km/s eastwards).

steps.title: Solved example: payload impact
steps.body: A 2% Δv shortfall corresponds to a payload loss of several percent (the payload-fraction curve is steep): r₂ is raised by reducing payload m_pl or structural mass m_s.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the orbital speed as the budget without losses.
- Ignoring the Earth's rotation benefit and launch azimuth constraints.
- Using vacuum I_sp for the first stage (use a sea-level/average value).

a.text: Your two-stage design's total Δv is 8,560 m/s but the mission needs about 8,720 m/s. What do you do first?

choices.label: Re-check I_sp (sea-level vs vacuum), losses estimate and mass ratios; then look for a small mass-ratio increase in stage 2
choices.feedback: Right: confirm the numbers and then make the cheapest change.

choices.label: Announce the design is fine because the difference is only 2%
choices.feedback: A 2% Δv shortfall can mean failing to reach orbit; margins must be positive.

choices.label: Double the first-stage propellant immediately
choices.feedback: A big change without analysis; stage 1 additions are far less effective per kg than stage 2 reductions in dead mass.

b.text: Increasing stage 2 mass ratio from 5.0 to 5.5 gives Δv₂ = 5,684 m/s and a total of 8,878 m/s. What is the margin and what should you do next?

choices.label: Margin ≈ 158 m/s (+1.8%); check payload mass and structural limits, then run a trajectory simulation with the real losses
choices.feedback: Correct: close the Δv budget, then verify with a full trajectory and structural analysis.

choices.label: Stop: the margin is positive so the design is finished
choices.feedback: Δv closure is only the first screen; trajectory, loads and reliability analyses remain.

x1.text: The rocket fails to reach orbit in the simulation. Re-run with a proper budget.

x2.text: The change adds mass and cost with little gain. Go back to analysing mass ratios.

x3.text: Later analysis shows the structure is overloaded during max-q. A budget is not a design.

end1.text: The design now closes with a positive margin and proceeds to detailed trajectory and structural analysis.

courses.summary: Formula sheet for aircraft propulsion, standard laboratory experiments (gas-turbine test bed, propeller static thrust, solid-rocket static firing) with observation tables and viva questions, previous-year-style problems and a 20-question exam. Independent study material.
outcomes: Recall key propulsion formulas
Reduce data from jet-engine, propeller and rocket-motor tests
Answer typical viva questions
Solve exam-style numericals on cycles, nozzles, turbomachinery and rockets

lessons.title: Formula and key-point sheet

scenes.text: The external examiner asks for the thrust equation, the Brayton efficiency and the rocket equation in ten minutes.
A compact sheet lets you answer all three.

steps.title: Air-breathing engines
steps.body:
- F = ṁ[(1+f)V_e − V₀] + (p_e − p₀)A_e; TSFC = ṁ_f/F; η_o = F V₀/(ṁ_f LHV) = η_th η_p; η_p ≈ 2/(1 + V_e/V₀).
- Brayton: η = 1 − r_p^{−(γ−1)/γ}; w_net max at T₂ = √(T₁T₃).
- T₀ = T(1 + 0.2M²); p₀ = p(1 + 0.2M²)^3.5.
- Compressor: T₀₃ = T₀₂[1 + (π^{0.2857} − 1)/η_c]; turbine: η_m c_p,t ΔT_t = c_p,c ΔT_c.
- f = c_p ΔT₀/(η_b LHV); choked nozzle: p₀₅/p₀ > 1.85–1.89; p*/p₀₅ = 0.528 (γ=1.4).
- Breguet: R = (V/c)(L/D)ln(W₀/W₁), c = TSFC·g.

steps.title: Turbomachinery, propellers, ramjets
steps.body:
- Euler: w = U Δc_θ; de Haller w₂/w₁ ≥ 0.72; R = (c_a/2U)(tanβ₁ + tanβ₂); π_s = [1 + η ΔT₀/T₀₁]^{3.5}.
- Centrifugal: w = σU₂², σ = 1 − 0.63π/Z.
- Corrected flow ṁ√θ/δ; surge margin = (π_surge − π_op)/π_op.
- Propeller: J = V/(nD); C_T = T/(ρn²D⁴); C_P = P/(ρn³D⁵); η = J C_T/C_P; ideal η_i = 2/(1 + V_e/V₀).
- Ramjet: T₉ = T₀₄/(1 + 0.2M₀²); F/ṁ = V₉ − V₀; zero static thrust.

steps.title: Rockets
steps.body:
- F = ṁV_e + (p_e − p_a)A_e; I_sp = F/(ṁ g₀); c = I_sp g₀.
- Δv = c ln(m₀/m_f); r = (1 + π_u)/(ε + π_u).
- V_e = √{(2γ/(γ−1)) R T_c[1 − (p_e/p_c)^{(γ−1)/γ}]}; c* = p_c A_t/ṁ; C_F = F/(p_c A_t); r_b = a p_c^n.
- Orbit speed v_c = √(μ/r), μ = 3.986×10¹⁴ m³/s².

steps.title: Top mistakes
steps.body:
- Missing the ram-drag term ṁV₀.
- Using γ = 1.4 for the hot section.
- Forgetting g₀ in the rocket equation.
- Using rpm instead of rev/s in propeller coefficients.

cards.back: η_o = η_th η_p = F V₀/(ṁ_f LHV)

lessons.title: Lab: Performance test of a small gas-turbine (turbojet) test bed

scenes.text: A small research turbojet is run on a thrust stand in a university test cell; ear defenders are mandatory.
You record thrust, fuel flow, temperatures and pressures at stepped speeds.

steps.title: Aim, apparatus, safety
steps.body:
**Aim**: to determine thrust, TSFC and thermal efficiency of a small turbojet at various rpm and to plot thrust vs rpm.
**Apparatus**: engine on a load-cell thrust stand, fuel flow meter, rpm sensor, thermocouples (T₀₃, T₀₅, exhaust), pressure transducers, intake bellmouth with static tap for air mass flow, noise protection.
**Procedure**: record ambient p and T; start and warm up per the manual; step rpm up at stable points (60%, 80%, 100%); log data for 30 s each; cool down; shut down. **Safety**: exhaust danger zone, FOD, fire extinguisher, emergency fuel shut-off, hearing protection.

steps.title: Observation table (bench, V₀ = 0, ambient 300 K, 100 kPa)
Sources of error
steps.body: Thrust-stand friction and drift, ambient wind over the intake, temperature effects on the load cell, fuel density variation, transient readings.

lessons.title: Lab: Static thrust of a propeller (with viva)

story.title: A drone propeller on the bench

scenes.text: A student team characterises a 10-inch propeller for a quadcopter.
The viva will ask why thrust scales with the square of speed.

steps.title: Aim and procedure
steps.body:
**Aim**: to measure static thrust at different speeds and compute the thrust coefficient C_T = T/(ρ n² D⁴).
**Apparatus**: propeller (D = 0.254 m), motor, load cell, tachometer, ESC, anemometer, thermometer/barometer.
**Procedure**: mount, zero the load cell, step the throttle, record n and T at stable points, repeat three times, compute averages. Air density from ρ = p/(RT) = 1.2 kg/m³ (at 100 kPa, 290 K).

steps.title: Sources of error
steps.body: Ground effect (keep the propeller at least one diameter from surfaces), recirculation, balance vibration, battery voltage sag.

activity.prompt: Typical viva questions with model answers.

items.q: Why does thrust scale as n²?
items.a: At a fixed advance ratio (J = 0) the blade section speeds scale with n D, so lift ∝ ρ(nD)²D² ∝ n².

items.q: What is the advance ratio at the static condition?
items.a: J = 0, since V₀ = 0.

items.q: Why is static thrust highest but efficiency zero?
items.a: Useful power T V₀ = 0 at V₀ = 0 while the power input is not.

items.q: What is the effect of ground proximity on thrust?
items.a: Ground effect increases thrust (reduced induced velocity) and distorts readings.

items.q: Why does a bigger, slower propeller give more thrust per watt?
items.a: Momentum theory: ideal power ∝ T^{3/2}/√(2ρA); larger A lowers power for the same thrust.

items.q: How does the propeller change at high flight speed?
items.a: J rises, thrust falls, pitch must be increased; at high Mach the tip compressibility drops efficiency.

lessons.title: Lab: Static firing of a solid rocket motor – impulse and I_sp

story.title: A model rocket motor on the test stand

scenes.text: A club range officer tests a model rocket motor in a remote, protected stand before certification.
The thrust–time curve gives total impulse and I_sp.

steps.title: Aim and theory
steps.body:
**Aim**: determine the thrust–time curve, total impulse, average thrust, burn time and I_sp of a small solid motor.
**Theory**: I_t = ∫F dt; F_avg = I_t/t_b; **I_sp = I_t/(m_p g₀)**. Letter classes of model motors double in total impulse per letter (e.g. an H motor is 160–320 N·s).
**Safety**: this is done only by authorised personnel on a certified range, with remote ignition, blast barrier and clear safety distances; do not attempt it at home.

steps.title: Sources of error
steps.body: Thrust-stand dynamics at ignition, sampling rate, case-insulation mass included in m_p, nozzle erosion, motor temperature effect on burn rate.

activity.prompt: From the table, I_sp = I_t/(m_p g₀) with I_t = 301.4 N·s and m_p = 0.30 kg (s).

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – Previous-year-style problem set

story.title: Four problems for the viva and the paper

scenes.text: A typical propulsion paper mixes one cycle problem, one turbomachinery, one propeller/ramjet and one rocket.
Do the ones you know first and show formulae.

steps.title: Problem 1 – turbojet (original)
steps.body:
A turbojet flies at 200 m/s at sea level, ṁ_a = 40 kg/s, V_e = 550 m/s, f = 0.02, fully expanded. Find thrust, TSFC and propulsive efficiency (exact form η_p = F V₀/ΔKĖ).
**Solution**: F = 40[(1.02)(550) − 200] = 40(561 − 200) = **14,440 N**; ṁ_f = 0.8 kg/s → TSFC = 0.8/14,440 = **5.54×10⁻⁵ kg/(N·s)**; ΔKĖ = ½[40.8×550² − 40×200²] = ½[12.342×10⁶ − 1.6×10⁶] = 5.371 MW; thrust power = 14,440×200 = 2.888 MW → **η_p = 0.538**.

steps.title: Problem 4 – rocket (original)
steps.body:
A stage has I_sp = 320 s, m₀ = 12,000 kg, m_f = 2,500 kg. Find Δv and burn time at ṁ = 50 kg/s.
**Solution**: Δv = 320×9.80665×ln(4.8) = 3,138×1.5686 = **4,922 m/s**; propellant 9,500 kg → t_b = **190 s**.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Write the governing equation first, list given data in SI units and give the answer with units. Cross-check with limiting cases.

lessons.title: Aircraft materials and the stress–strain relation

story.title: Why aeroplanes are not made of steel

scenes.text: A 5 mm sheet of steel is three times heavier than the same aluminium sheet, yet an aircraft has to be as light as safety allows.
Structural engineers pick materials by strength/weight and stiffness/weight, not by strength alone.

steps.title: Hooke's law and properties
steps.body:
For axial loading: **σ = P/A** (Pa), **ε = ΔL/L**, **σ = Eε** in the elastic range, with Poisson's ratio ν = −ε_lateral/ε_axial. Shear: τ = Gγ, **G = E/(2(1 + ν))**. Key properties: modulus E, yield strength σ_y (0.2% proof), ultimate σ_u, elongation, fracture toughness K_IC, fatigue strength, density ρ.

Typical values (rounded; check material specifications for design):
- **Aluminium 2024-T3**: E ≈ 73 GPa, σ_y ≈ 345 MPa, σ_u ≈ 483 MPa, ρ ≈ 2,780 kg/m³ (fuselage skin, damage tolerant).
- **Aluminium 7075-T6**: E ≈ 72 GPa, σ_y ≈ 500 MPa, σ_u ≈ 570 MPa, ρ ≈ 2,810 (wing upper skin, high strength).
- **Titanium Ti-6Al-4V**: E ≈ 114 GPa, σ_y ≈ 880 MPa, ρ ≈ 4,430.
- **Steel (high strength)**: E ≈ 200 GPa, ρ ≈ 7,850 (landing gear).
- **CFRP (unidirectional, along fibre)**: E ≈ 135–180 GPa, ρ ≈ 1,550 (modern wings and fuselages).

Specific stiffness E/ρ and specific strength σ/ρ rank materials by weight efficiency.

steps.title: Solved example: axial member
steps.body: Aluminium strut (E = 72 GPa), area 100 mm², length 1 m, load 20 kN: σ = 20,000/100×10⁻⁶ = 200 MPa; ε = 200/72,000 = 0.002778; ΔL = 2.78 mm. Yield margin: 345/200 = 1.7.

steps.title: Solved example: specific stiffness
steps.body: E/ρ: Al 2024: 73×10⁹/2780 = 26.3 MJ/kg; Ti: 114×10⁹/4430 = 25.7 MJ/kg; steel 200×10⁹/7850 = 25.5; CFRP 150×10⁹/1550 = 96.8 MJ/kg. Metals are almost equal in specific stiffness: composites are about 3–4 times better in the fibre direction.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the yield stress as allowable ultimate stress (or the opposite).
- Mixing MPa and N/m².
- Forgetting that composites are anisotropic: E depends on direction.

activity.prompt: Aluminium strut: A = 100 mm², L = 1 m, E = 72 GPa, load 20 kN. Elongation in mm.

lessons.title: Lab: Stress transformation and Mohr's circle

story.title: What is the real peak stress?

scenes.text: A strain-gauge rosette on a wing skin gives σx, σy and τxy. The maximum stress may act on a different plane.
Mohr's circle finds it graphically and analytically.

steps.title: Equations
steps.body:
For plane stress (σx, σy, τxy) on a plane rotated by θ:

σ_θ = (σx + σy)/2 + ((σx − σy)/2) cos2θ + τxy sin2θ
τ_θ = −((σx − σy)/2) sin2θ + τxy cos2θ

**Principal stresses**: σ₁,₂ = (σx + σy)/2 ± R, with **R = √(((σx − σy)/2)² + τxy²)** = τ_max (in-plane). Principal angle: **tan2θ_p = 2τxy/(σx − σy)**. Mohr's circle: centre C = (σx + σy)/2 on the σ-axis, radius R; points (σx, τxy) and (σy, −τxy) are the ends of a diameter.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
σx = 100 MPa, σy = −40 MPa, τxy = 30 MPa.
C = 30 MPa; (σx − σy)/2 = 70; R = √(70² + 30²) = **76.16 MPa**.
σ₁ = 30 + 76.16 = **106.2 MPa**; σ₂ = 30 − 76.16 = **−46.2 MPa**.
tan2θ_p = 60/140 = 0.4286 → 2θ_p = 23.2°, **θ_p = 11.6°** (σ₁ direction).
τ_max = 76.2 MPa on planes 45° from the principal planes.

steps.title: Solved example: pure shear
steps.body: σx = σy = 0, τxy = 50: R = 50, σ₁ = +50, σ₂ = −50 at 45°: a shear-loaded skin panel carries tension along one diagonal and compression along the other (this is why shear panels buckle in diagonal waves).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using θ instead of 2θ in the circle.
- Sign convention for τ: be consistent (clockwise-positive on Mohr's circle).
- Forgetting the out-of-plane principal stress (0) when finding the absolute maximum shear.

activity.prompt: σx = 100, σy = −40, τxy = 30 MPa. Find the larger principal stress σ₁ (MPa).
