lessons.title: Lab: Yield criteria – Tresca and von Mises

scenes.text: A combined-stress state cannot be compared directly with a tensile test yield stress.
A yield criterion converts it to an equivalent stress.

steps.title: Criteria for ductile metals
steps.body:
- **Maximum shear stress (Tresca)**: yield when τ_max = σ_y/2, i.e. **σ₁ − σ₃ = σ_y** (σ₁ ≥ σ₂ ≥ σ₃, include σ = 0 out of plane).
- **Von Mises (distortion energy)**: yield when **σ_vm = √(σ₁² − σ₁σ₂ + σ₂²) = σ_y** (plane stress). In general σ_vm = √(½[(σ₁−σ₂)² + (σ₂−σ₃)² + (σ₃−σ₁)²]).
Tresca is slightly conservative; von Mises fits test data better (difference up to 15%).
- Brittle materials: maximum principal stress (Rankine) or Mohr–Coulomb.
- Composites: Tsai–Wu, Tsai–Hill, maximum strain criteria (Unit 6).

steps.title: Solved example: thin pressurised cylinder
steps.body: Fuselage radius r = 1.8 m, skin t = 1.5 mm, cabin differential pressure Δp = 60 kPa: hoop σ_h = Δp r/t = 60,000×1.8/0.0015 = **72 MPa**; longitudinal σ_L = Δp r/(2t) = **36 MPa**. von Mises: √(72² − 72×36 + 36²) = √(5184 − 2592 + 1296) = √3888 = **62.4 MPa**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using σ_vm formula with absolute values instead of signed principal stresses.
- Forgetting that cabin pressurisation cycles drive fatigue, not just static stress.
- Applying von Mises to wrinkled/buckled skin.

activity.prompt: Plane stress σ₁ = 106.2 MPa, σ₂ = −46.2 MPa. Von Mises stress (MPa).

quiz.q: Hoop stress for Δp = 60 kPa, r = 1.8 m, t = 1.5 mm

lessons.title: Lab: Flight loads – load factor, V–n diagram and gusts

story.title: How strong must the wing be?

scenes.text: A certification engineer asks what maximum load factor the wing must carry in a turn, a pull-up, or a gust.
The answer defines the design loads for every structural member.

steps.title: Load factor and the V–n diagram
steps.body:
**Load factor n = L/W** (g). Limit load = highest load expected in service; **ultimate load = 1.5 × limit** (factor of safety 1.5 for the aircraft certification rules (CS-23/25, FAR 23/25): the structure must support limit load without permanent deformation and ultimate load for 3 s without failure).

- Level turn at bank φ: **n = 1/cosφ** (60° → n = 2).
- Pull-up in a circle of radius R at speed V: **n = 1 + V²/(gR)**.
- Aerodynamic limit: **n = ½ρV²S CLmax/W = (V/V_s)²** (parabola on the V–n diagram).
- **Manoeuvre speed V_A = V_s √n_lim**: the highest speed at which a full-deflection stall does not exceed n_lim.
- Limit load factors: transport aircraft +2.5 to −1.0; normal-category light aircraft up to +3.8; aerobatic +6.
- **Gust load factor**: Δn = ρ V a K_g U_de S/(2W) (V in EAS), with a = CLα, K_g the gust alleviation factor, U_de derived gust velocity (e.g. 15.2 m/s).

steps.title: Solved example: V–n corner
steps.body: W = 12,000 N, S = 16 m², CLmax = 1.6, sea level: V_s = √(2×12,000/(1.225×16×1.6)) = √765.3 = 27.66 m/s. With n_lim = 3.8: V_A = 27.66×√3.8 = 27.66×1.949 = **53.9 m/s**. At V = 60 m/s the aerodynamic limit n = (60/27.66)² = 4.70 > 3.8: a pilot can exceed the limit load if he pulls hard → a V_A placard.

steps.title: Solved example: pull-up and gust
steps.body:
(a) Pull-up at V = 100 m/s, R = 500 m: n = 1 + 10,000/(500×9.81) = **3.04**.
(b) Gust at 60 m/s, a = 5.0/rad, K_g = 0.8, U_de = 15.2 m/s: Δn = 1.225×60×5.0×0.8×15.2×16/(2×12,000) = **2.98**, so the gust load factor n ≈ 3.98 > 3.8 — gust may be critical for light aircraft.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using ultimate = limit instead of 1.5×limit.
- Applying n = 1/cosφ for non-level turns.
- Using TAS rather than EAS in gust formulas.

activity.prompt: W = 12,000 N, S = 16 m², CLmax = 1.6, sea level, limit load factor 3.8. Find the manoeuvre speed V_A (m/s).

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – Margin of safety of a wing-fitting lug

story.title: The pin that holds the strut

scenes.text: A wing strut attaches to the spar through a simple lug and pin.
You check net-section tension, bearing and compute the margin of safety.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
For a lug of width w, hole diameter d, thickness t, pin load P:
- **Net-section tension**: σ_net = P/((w − d)t). (Real lugs add a stress-concentration/efficiency factor K_t; this is a simplified estimate.)
- **Bearing**: σ_b = P/(d t).
- **Margin of safety MS = allowable/(applied) − 1**; applied loads are ultimate (1.5 × limit); MS ≥ 0 is acceptable.
- Shear-out / tear-out also checked for edge distance e: τ = P/(2 e t).

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Limit pin load P = 25 kN; ultimate = 37.5 kN. 2024-T3 lug: w = 40 mm, d = 12 mm, t = 4 mm.
Net area = (40 − 12)×4 = 112 mm²: σ_net(ultimate) = 37,500/112 = **334.8 MPa**; allowable σ_u = 483 MPa → **MS = 483/334.8 − 1 = 0.44**.
Bearing at ultimate: 37,500/(12×4) = 781 MPa — bearing allowables for lugs are higher (≈ 1.5–2× σ_u), check with the proper data.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using limit load with the ultimate allowable (inconsistent factor).
- Ignoring stress concentration at the hole and fatigue.
- Checking only tension: shear-out and bearing may govern.

lessons.title: Lab: Bending stress in a wing-spar I-section

story.title: Why spars look like the letter I

scenes.text: A wing spar carries bending from lift: material far from the neutral axis does the work.
You compute the second moment of area and the peak stress.

steps.title: Pure bending theory
steps.body:
Assumptions (Euler–Bernoulli): plane sections remain plane; linear elastic; small deflections. Then **σ = M y / I**, where I = ∫y² dA (mm⁴), y measured from the neutral axis (centroid). Curvature **1/R = M/(EI)**; deflection: EI d²v/dx² = M(x). Parallel-axis theorem: **I = I_c + A d²**. Section modulus Z = I/y_max.

For a thin-walled I-beam with flanges (b × t_f) and web (t_w × h_w) the flange contribution dominates; this is why the web is thin and flanges (caps) are thick.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
I-section: flanges 50 × 5 mm, web 4 mm thick, clear height 100 mm (overall depth 110 mm). Flange centroid at y = 52.5 mm.
I = 2[50×5³/12 + (50×5)(52.5)²] + 4×100³/12 = 2[520.8 + 689,062.5] + 333,333 = **1.7125×10⁶ mm⁴**.
M = 5 kN·m = 5×10⁶ N·mm: σ_max = 5×10⁶×55/1.7125×10⁶ = **160.6 MPa** (tension at bottom, compression at top).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the web height instead of the flange centroid distance.
- Forgetting the parallel-axis term.
- Using mm and m together.

activity.prompt: I-section: I = 1.7125×10⁶ mm⁴, M = 5×10⁶ N·mm, y_max = 55 mm. Peak bending stress (MPa).

options: they are far from the neutral axis

lessons.title: Unsymmetric bending

story.title: The load is not along a principal axis

scenes.text: A rectangular strut is loaded by a force inclined 30° to its web axis.
The neutral axis is not along the load direction.

steps.title: Principal axes method
steps.body:
Resolve the bending moment along the section's principal axes (x, y) with second moments I_x, I_y (I_xy = 0): **σ = M_x y/I_x + M_y x/I_y** (signs by convention). The neutral axis (σ = 0) satisfies y/x = −(M_y I_x)/(M_x I_y), so it is not parallel to the moment vector unless I_x = I_y.

General axes (with product I_xy): **σ = [(M_x I_y − M_y I_xy) y + (M_y I_x − M_x I_xy) x]/(I_x I_y − I_xy²)**. For Z, L and unsymmetric sections, product of inertia matters. For thin-walled sections the product I_xy = ∫xy dA.

steps.title: Solved example: rectangle
steps.body:
Section b = 20 mm (x), h = 60 mm (y): I_x = 20×60³/12 = 360,000 mm⁴; I_y = 60×20³/12 = 40,000 mm⁴. Moment M = 100 N·m = 10⁵ N·mm in a plane at 30° to the y axis: M_x = 10⁵ cos30° = 86,603; M_y = 10⁵ sin30° = 50,000.
Corner (x = 10, y = 30): σ = 86,603×30/360,000 + 50,000×10/40,000 = 7.22 + 12.50 = **19.72 MPa**.
Neutral axis: tanα = (I_x/I_y) tanφ = 9×0.577 = 5.20 → α = 79.1° from the x axis: it lies much closer to the weak axis, showing how sensitive a slender section is to small lateral loads.

steps.title: Solved example: comparison with the aligned case
steps.body: If the same moment were purely about x: σ = 10⁵×30/360,000 = 8.33 MPa. A 30° tilt more than doubles the peak stress (19.7 vs 8.3).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the full moment with only I_x.
- Taking the neutral axis along the load line.
- Ignoring I_xy for Z and angle sections.

lessons.title: Lab: Shear flow and shear stress in thin-walled open sections

scenes.text: A shear force on a channel makes the web carry most of it and the flanges carry shear flow that varies along their length.
Shear flow q (N/mm) is the shear force per unit length along the wall.

steps.title: Shear flow formula
steps.body:
For a thin-walled open section with shear S_y through the shear centre (symmetric about the x axis, or principal axes):

**q(s) = −(S_y/I_xx) ∫₀^s t y ds** (N/mm), **τ = q/t**.

The integral Q(s) = ∫ t y ds is the first moment of area of the portion beyond s. Properties: q = 0 at free edges; q is continuous at junctions (**q-in = q-out** for a branch); the resultant of q over the wall equals S_y; shear flow is largest near the neutral axis. Direction: from the free edge toward the web.

steps.title: Solved example: channel
steps.body:
Channel: flanges b = 50 mm, web h = 100 mm, thickness t = 2 mm. I_xx = 2×100³/12 + 2×(50×2)(50)² = 166,667 + 500,000 = **666,667 mm⁴**. S = 20 kN: S/I = 0.03 N/mm⁴.
Flange: q(s) = 0.03×2×50×s = 3s → at the corner s = 50: **q = 150 N/mm** (τ = 75 MPa).
Web at the neutral axis: 150 + 0.03×2×50²/2 = 150 + 75 = **225 N/mm** (τ = 112.5 MPa).

steps.title: Solved example: check by resultant
steps.body: Web force = ∫q dy = 0.03 ∫(7500 − y²) dy over ±50 = 0.03×(750,000 − 83,333) = **20,000 N = S** ✓. The flanges' shear flows form two horizontal forces of 0.5×150×50 = 3,750 N each, equal and opposite (giving a torque, see next lesson).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the total area instead of the area beyond the cut.
- Ignoring the sign (direction) of q.
- Applying the formula when the load does not pass through the shear centre (the section will also twist).

lessons.title: Lab: Shear centre of a channel section

scenes.text: Load a channel through the web and it twists; there is one point through which a load causes pure bending without twist.
That point is the shear centre, and wings are designed so that lift acts near it.

steps.title: Definition and method
steps.body:
The **shear centre** (flexural centre) is the point in the section through which a transverse shear force must act to produce no twist. Procedure: (1) find shear flows; (2) resultants of flange and web forces; (3) take moments about a convenient point (e.g. the web) and equate to S × e.

For a channel with uniform thickness, flange width b (from web centreline), web height h: **e = 3b²/(h + 6b)** measured from the web centreline. The shear centre lies on the axis of symmetry, outside the web, on the side away from the flange tips.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: b = 50 mm, h = 100 mm, t = 2 mm, I = 666,667 mm⁴, S = 20 kN. Flange force F = ½ q_corner b = ½×150×50 = 3,750 N. Moments about the web: S e = F h = 3,750×100 → **e = 3,750×100/20,000 = 18.75 mm**. Check with the formula: 3×50²/(100 + 300) = 7,500/400 = **18.75 mm** ✓.

steps.title: Solved example: torque from eccentric load
steps.body: If the 20 kN load is applied in the plane of the web (distance e = 18.75 mm from the shear centre), the section is loaded by a torque T = 20,000×18.75 = **375,000 N·mm = 375 N·m** in addition to bending. For a wing this means that the lift acting at the aerodynamic centre, not at the shear centre of the box, twists the wing.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Taking moments about different points inconsistently.
- Placing the shear centre on the centroid: only true for doubly symmetric sections.
- Forgetting that the shear centre depends only on geometry, not on loading.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – Idealised boom-and-web wing beam

story.title: How stress engineers simplify a wing

scenes.text: Real wing boxes have stringers, skin and spars. Stress engineers idealise them as booms (carry direct stress) and webs (carry only shear).
The idealisation makes hand checks quick.

steps.title: Idealisation
steps.body:
- **Booms** of area B_r carry all direct stress: σ_r = M y_r/I with I = Σ B_r y_r².
- **Webs/skin panels** are assumed to carry only shear flow, constant between booms.
- Change in shear flow across a boom: **Δq = −(S_y/I_xx) B_r y_r**.

For a two-boom beam (flanges separated by h): the web carries **q = S/h**; boom load = M/h.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Two booms B = 400 mm² each at y = ±100 mm (h = 200 mm): I_xx = 2×400×100² = **8.0×10⁶ mm⁴**. Loads: M = 10 kN·m, S = 20 kN.
Boom stress σ = 10⁷×100/8×10⁶ = **125 MPa** (boom force 50,000 N = M/h ✓).
Web shear flow q = S B y/I = 20,000×400×100/8×10⁶ = **100 N/mm** = S/h ✓; τ_web (t = 1.5 mm) = 66.7 MPa.

steps.title: Solved example: four-boom box
steps.body: Booms (area 300 mm² each) at (±150, ±50) mm: I_xx = 4×300×50² = 3.0×10⁶ mm⁴. S = 15 kN through the shear centre: change of q across each boom = (15,000/3×10⁶)×300×50 = **75 N/mm**. Top web (between top booms) carries q₀ and the vertical webs carry q₀ ± 75: the open section is solved from the free edge; for closed boxes the constant q₀ comes from the torsion/twist condition (Unit 3).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Letting the web carry bending stress (not allowed in the idealisation unless its area is lumped into the booms).
- Using an inconsistent boom area (lump half of the adjoining web's contribution: B = A_s + (t_b/6)(2 + σ₂/σ₁) etc.).
- Forgetting to check buckling of the thin webs (Unit 5).

courses.summary: Torsion of closed thin-walled sections (Bredt–Batho), open-section torsion, multicell boxes, wing-box torsional stiffness and combined shear/torsion in a boom–web box. Covers topics commonly taught in Indian B.Tech aerospace programmes.

lessons.title: Lab: Torsion of a closed thin-walled section (Bredt–Batho)

scenes.text: A closed box twists far less than an open channel of the same material.
You derive the shear flow and the twist rate of a single-cell section.

steps.title: Bredt–Batho theory
steps.body:
For a single-cell thin-walled closed section under torque T (no axial restraint): shear flow **q = const around the cell**. Moment about any point: T = ∮ q p ds = q ∮ p ds = **2 A q**, where A is the area enclosed by the wall mid-line. Hence **q = T/(2A)**, **τ = T/(2At)**; the maximum shear stress occurs in the thinnest wall.

**Twist**: strain energy ⇒ **dθ/dz = (q/(2AG)) ∮ ds/t = T ∮ ds/t /(4A²G)**. Torsion constant **J = 4A²/∮(ds/t)** (so T = GJ dθ/dz). For a tube of uniform t: J = 4A²t/perimeter.

steps.title: Solved example: varying thickness
steps.body: If the top and bottom skins are 2 mm and the webs 1.5 mm: ∮ds/t = 2×300/2 + 2×100/1.5 = 300 + 133.3 = 433.3. J = 4×(30,000)²/433.3 = 8.31×10⁶ mm⁴. q is unchanged (T/2A) but τ is highest in the 1.5 mm webs (22.2 MPa vs 16.7 MPa in the skins).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the outer area instead of the mid-line enclosed area.
- Using the Bredt formula for open sections (use the J = Σ bt³/3 rule instead).
- Forgetting that restrained warping changes the stress near the root.

lessons.title: Lab: Open versus closed sections in torsion

story.title: Slit a tube and it becomes floppy

scenes.text: Twist a cardboard tube, then slit it along its length and twist again: the slit tube is dramatically softer.
You quantify the difference.

steps.title: Open thin-walled sections
steps.body:
For an open section of narrow rectangles (b_i × t_i): **J = (1/3) Σ b_i t_i³**; **τ_max = T t_max/J**; **dθ/dz = T/(GJ)**. The shear stress flows around within the thickness (it is zero on the mid-line). Because t³ is small, J is tiny: open sections are poor in torsion.

Closed vs open (same area of metal, same material): the closed tube has J_closed/J_open ≈ 3(r/t)² for a circular tube (r mean radius): for r/t = 20, ratio = 1,200.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Strip 100 mm × 2 mm, G = 27 GPa, T = 10 N·m = 10⁴ N·mm. J = ⅓×100×2³ = 266.7 mm⁴. τ_max = 10⁴×2/266.7 = **75 MPa**; dθ/dz = 10⁴/(27,000×266.7) = 1.389×10⁻³ rad/mm = **79.6°/m**.
Close the strip into a circular tube (perimeter 100 mm, r = 15.9 mm, A = 796 mm², t = 2 mm): q = T/2A = 6.28 N/mm, τ = **3.14 MPa**: 24 times lower stress. J_closed = 4A²/(100/2) = 5.07×10⁴ mm⁴ (190× stiffer).

steps.title: Solved example: angle section
steps.body: Angle with legs 50 × 3 mm and 40 × 3 mm: J = ⅓(50 + 40)×27 = **810 mm⁴**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the closed-section formula on open sections.
- Forgetting that J ∝ t³.
- Neglecting that, for built-up wings, the skin must be closed (a lap/rivet line is closed if shear can pass).

lessons.title: Lab: Two-cell sections and equal twist

story.title: The wing box with a centre spar

scenes.text: A multi-spar wing box is a multicell section: shear flows must satisfy equilibrium and equal twist in each cell.
You solve a two-cell box.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
For N cells under torque T: unknowns q₁…q_N (cell circulating shear flows); the shared wall carries the difference.
- **Equilibrium**: T = Σ 2A_i q_i.
- **Compatibility** (equal twist rate): dθ/dz = (1/(2A_i G)) ∮ q ds/t, the same for all cells (N − 1 equations).
Solve the linear system.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Two cells with a common web 150 mm: cell 1: 200 × 150 (A₁ = 30,000 mm²); cell 2: 100 × 150 (A₂ = 15,000 mm²); t = 2 mm everywhere; T = 5×10⁶ N·mm.
Cell 1 perimeter 700 mm; cell 2: 500 mm; common web 150 mm.
Twist: (700q₁ − 150q₂)/A₁ = (500q₂ − 150q₁)/A₂ → (700q₁ − 150q₂)/30,000 = (500q₂ − 150q₁)/15,000 → 1000q₁ = 1150q₂ → **q₁ = 1.15 q₂**.
Torque: 5×10⁶ = 2×30,000(1.15q₂) + 2×15,000 q₂ = 99,000 q₂ → **q₂ = 50.5 N/mm**, **q₁ = 58.1 N/mm**; the common web carries q₁ − q₂ = **7.6 N/mm**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting that the common web is traversed in opposite directions by the two cells.
- Using a single area for the whole section.
- Missing a compatibility equation.

lessons.title: Lab: Torsional stiffness and twist of a wing box

scenes.text: Lift acting aft of the shear centre twists a wing nose-up (increasing lift) - a feedback that can lead to divergence.
The wing's GJ sets the twist.

steps.title: Wing twist
steps.body:
For a wing box with torque T(z) along the span: **θ(z) = ∫ T/(GJ) dz**. A wing generating lift L′ per unit span at a distance e_a from the shear centre produces T′ = L′ e_a. For constant T over a length L: **θ = TL/(GJ)**.

Design consequences: (1) aeroelastic divergence speed ∝ √(GJ/e); (2) aileron reversal; (3) washout from bending–torsion coupling in swept wings; (4) torsional stiffness is increased by closing the box, adding spars, and thick skins on the closed cell.

steps.title: Solved example: effect of a thinner skin
steps.body: If the skin is 1 mm thick instead of 2 mm, ∮ds/t doubles to 1100 and J halves: θ = 0.486°. Doubling the box depth from 150 to 300 mm increases A to 120,000 mm² (×2) and ∮ds/t = 1400/2 = 700: J = 4×(1.2×10⁵)²/700 = 8.23×10⁷ mm⁴ (3.1×). Depth is the most effective way to increase J.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the aerodynamic chord instead of the box dimensions.
- Ignoring cut-outs: access panels reduce J substantially.
- Ignoring warping restraint at the root.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – Shear flow in a boom box with an off-centre load

story.title: A flap hinge pulls the box sideways

scenes.text: A flap-track fitting applies a 10 kN vertical load 50 mm off the shear centre of a wing box.
You compute the webs' shear flows from bending shear plus torsion.

steps.title: Method
steps.body: Resolve the load into (a) the same force S acting through the shear centre (pure bending shear) and (b) a torque T = S × e. Superpose the shear flows: **q = q_S + q_T**, with q_T = T/(2A) circulating around the cell.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Rectangular box 300 mm wide × 100 mm high; 4 corner booms B = 500 mm²; thin webs carry shear only. I_xx = 4×500×50² = **5×10⁶ mm⁴**. S = 10 kN vertical, symmetric box: shear centre at mid-width (150 mm). Load acts at 100 mm from the left web: e = 50 mm.
(a) q_S: across each boom ΔS = S B y/I = 10,000×500×50/5×10⁶ = 50 N/mm; the vertical webs carry **50 N/mm** each (S/2h = 50 ✓), the horizontal webs 0.
(b) T = 10,000×50 = 5×10⁵ N·mm; A = 30,000 mm²: q_T = 5×10⁵/60,000 = **8.33 N/mm**.
(c) Total: one vertical web 50 + 8.33 = **58.3 N/mm**, the other 50 − 8.33 = **41.7 N/mm** (sum = 100 N/mm × 100 mm = 10 kN ✓); the horizontal webs carry 8.33 N/mm.

steps.title: Solved example: shear stress
steps.body: With web thickness 1.5 mm: τ = 58.3/1.5 = 38.9 MPa; 41.7/1.5 = 27.8 MPa. Compare with the shear buckling strength of the web (Unit 5).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding q_T and q_S with the wrong signs: the web on the side of the load takes more shear.
- Forgetting that the load location relative to the shear centre matters, not the centroid.
- Forgetting torsion in the horizontal webs.

courses.summary: Strain energy, Castigliano's theorems, the unit-load method for trusses and beams, statically indeterminate structures by the force method, beam deflections and a strut-braced wing capstone. Covers topics commonly taught in Indian B.Tech aerospace programmes.
outcomes: Compute strain energy for axial, bending, shear and torsion

lessons.title: Strain energy and Castigliano's theorems

scenes.text: A loaded structure behaves like a spring: the work done by the loads is stored as strain energy.
Differentiating that energy gives deflections without drawing deflected shapes.

steps.title: Strain energy expressions (linear elastic)
steps.body:
- Axial: **U = ∫ P²/(2AE) dx** (= P²L/2AE for constant load).
- Bending: **U = ∫ M²/(2EI) dx**.
- Torsion: **U = ∫ T²/(2GJ) dx**.
- Shear: **U = ∫ k S²/(2GA) dx** (k = form factor; often small for slender beams).

**Castigliano's second theorem**: deflection in the direction of the load Q_i is **δ_i = ∂U/∂Q_i** (apply a dummy load Q = 0 where no load acts, differentiate, then set Q = 0). Combined: δ = ∫ (M ∂M/∂P)/(EI) dx + ∫ (N ∂N/∂P)/(AE) dx + ∫ (T ∂T/∂P)/(GJ) dx.
**First theorem**: P_i = ∂U/∂δ_i. **Maxwell's reciprocity**: δ_ij = δ_ji.

steps.title: Solved example: dummy load
steps.body: A cantilever with UDL w has no point load at the tip. Add Q at the tip: M = −wx²/2 − Qx; ∂M/∂Q = −x. δ_tip = ∫(wx²/2)(x)/(EI) dx = wL⁴/(8EI) ✓.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Differentiating after substituting numbers (do it before setting Q = 0).
- Forgetting that the theorem gives the deflection *in the direction of the applied (or dummy) load*.
- Using strain energy for non-linear elastic behaviour.

activity.prompt: Cantilever tip deflection δ = PL³/(3EI): P = 1000 N, L = 1500 mm, E = 72,000 N/mm², I = 1.7125×10⁶ mm⁴. Give δ (mm).

options: no load at the point of interest

lessons.title: Lab: Unit-load method for pin-jointed trusses

story.title: How much does the roof sag?

scenes.text: A hangar roof truss is loaded at the apex, and the engineer must check the sag.
The unit-load method gives deflection in three lines.

steps.title: Method
steps.body: For a truss: **δ = Σ (F_i f_i L_i)/(A_i E_i)**, where F_i are member forces due to the real loads and f_i those due to a unit load at the point and direction of the desired deflection. Procedure: (1) find F by statics (method of joints or sections); (2) apply a unit load and find f; (3) tabulate; (4) sum. Tension positive.

steps.title: Solved example: two-bar truss
steps.body:
Supports A and B at the same level 4 m apart; apex C 2 m above the line AB; vertical load P = 20 kN at C. Members AC, BC: length 2.828 m at 45°. Each carries F = P/(2 sin45°) = 14.14 kN (compression: −14.14 kN); for a unit load f = −0.7071. A = 400 mm², E = 72 GPa → AE = 2.88×10⁷ N.
δ_C = 2×[(−14,142)(−0.7071)(2,828.4)]/(2.88×10⁷) = 2×2.828×10⁷/2.88×10⁷ = **1.96 mm** downward.

steps.title: Solved example: adding a tie
steps.body: If a third member is added from A to B (a tie), it carries the horizontal thrust and the truss becomes statically determinate if supported by a pin and a roller; the same unit-load procedure applies, now with a tie force F = P/2 × (span/(2×rise)) = 20,000/2 × 1 = 10 kN (tension).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing the sign of forces F and f.
- Using the real load when computing f (f is per unit load).
- Including zero-force members incorrectly: they contribute only if f ≠ 0 and F ≠ 0.

activity.prompt: Two-bar truss (above): δ_C = 2·F f L/(AE), F = 14,142 N, f = 0.7071, L = 2,828.4 mm, AE = 2.88×10⁷ N. Vertical deflection (mm).

options: may still deflect other joints if f≠0 and F≠0

lessons.title: Lab: Statically indeterminate structures – the force method

scenes.text: A wing carried by a root fitting and also a tip strut has more supports than statics can resolve.
Deflection compatibility provides the missing equation.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
Degree of indeterminacy = number of unknown reactions/forces − number of independent equilibrium equations. **Force (flexibility) method**: (1) remove redundant(s) to get a determinate 'primary' structure; (2) compute the deflection at the redundant due to the loads (δ₁₀) and due to a unit redundant (f₁₁); (3) enforce compatibility **δ₁₀ + X f₁₁ = 0** (or the support displacement); (4) solve X and superpose.

**Parallel load sharing**: members of equal length share load in proportion to their stiffness k = AE/L.

steps.title: Solved example: propped cantilever with UDL
steps.body: Fixed at x = 0, propped at x = L, uniform load w = 2 N/mm, L = 2,000 mm. Remove the prop (reaction R): tip deflection due to w: wL⁴/(8EI); due to R upward: RL³/(3EI). Compatibility: wL⁴/(8EI) = RL³/(3EI) → **R = 3wL/8 = 1,500 N**. Fixed-end moment = wL²/2 − RL = 4×10⁶ − 3×10⁶ = 1×10⁶ N·mm = **wL²/8**. (Without the prop the root moment would be wL²/2 = 4×10⁶ N·mm, so the prop cuts it by 75%.)

steps.title: Solved example: two parallel rods
steps.body: Aluminium rod A = 300 mm², E = 72 GPa and steel rod A = 100 mm², E = 200 GPa, same length, load P = 50 kN shared. k_Al = 21.6×10⁶/L, k_St = 20×10⁶/L → Al share = 21.6/41.6 = 51.9% → **25.96 kN**, steel 24.04 kN. Equal strain: σ_Al = 86.5 MPa, σ_St = 240 MPa.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Wrong sign of the redundant's displacement.
- Forgetting that indeterminate structures are sensitive to temperature, assembly errors and support settlement.
- Choosing a redundant that makes the primary structure unstable.

story.title: How far does the wing tip rise?

scenes.text: In flight a long wing flexes upward; a glider wing tip may rise 10% of its semi-span.
You estimate the tip deflection with the cantilever formulae.

steps.title: Standard results
steps.body:
EI v″ = M(x). Boundary conditions give:
- Cantilever, tip load P: **δ = PL³/(3EI)**, slope PL²/(2EI).
- Cantilever, UDL w: **δ = wL⁴/(8EI)**, slope wL³/(6EI).
- Simply supported, central load P: **δ = PL³/(48EI)**.
- Simply supported, UDL: **δ = 5wL⁴/(384EI)**.
- Cantilever with end moment M: δ = ML²/(2EI).
Macaulay's brackets handle several loads. For tapering wings, EI varies; use numerical integration or the unit-load method.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using w in N/m with L in mm.
- Confusing slope and deflection formulas.
- Using a constant EI on a strongly tapered wing.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – Strut-braced wing as an indeterminate structure

story.title: The strut that shares the load

scenes.text: A high-wing light aircraft braces each wing with a strut to the fuselage.
The strut takes part of the lift: how much depends on relative stiffness.

steps.title: Model
steps.body: Treat the wing as a cantilever with tip stiffness **k_b = 3EI/L³** and the strut (vertical for simplicity) with axial stiffness **k_s = AE/L_s**. Under a tip load P the strut force **R = P k_s/(k_s + k_b)**; the tip deflection is **δ = (P − R)/k_b = R/k_s**.

steps.title: Solved example: root moment reduction
steps.body: Unstrutted root moment = P L = 15 kN·m. With strut: (P − R)L = 1,538×3,000 = **4.6 kN·m**: the strut reduces the wing-root bending moment by 69%, at the price of a compression load in the strut on negative-g loading (buckling) and fuselage fitting loads.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the strut's inclined length for stiffness without the angle correction (k = AE cos²θ/L_s for vertical deflection).
- Ignoring the compression/buckling case of the strut in negative g.
- Treating the strut as rigid.

lessons.title: Lab: Euler column buckling

scenes.text: A slender wing-strut under compression does not fail by crushing: it suddenly bows sideways.
Euler found the critical load in 1744.

steps.title: Euler's formula
steps.body:
For a perfect, elastic, initially straight column with pinned ends, the equilibrium equation EI v″ + P v = 0 has a non-trivial solution v = A sin(πx/L) only when **P_cr = π²EI/L²**. In general **P_cr = π²EI/L_e²**, where the effective length **L_e = K L**: pinned–pinned K = 1; fixed–free K = 2; fixed–fixed K = 0.5; fixed–pinned K ≈ 0.7. The column buckles about the axis with the smallest I.

Critical stress **σ_cr = π²E/(L_e/r)²**, with radius of gyration r = √(I/A) and slenderness ratio λ = L_e/r. Valid only if σ_cr < proportional limit (long columns). Real columns with imperfections or eccentric loads fail at lower loads (Perry–Robertson, Southwell plot).

steps.title: Solved example: pinned rod
steps.body:
Aluminium rod (E = 72 GPa), d = 20 mm, L = 600 mm, pinned: I = πd⁴/64 = 7,854 mm⁴; A = 314.2 mm²; r = 5 mm; λ = 120.
P_cr = π²×72,000×7,854/600² = **15.5 kN**; σ_cr = 49.3 MPa ≪ σ_y = 345 MPa (elastic buckling).

steps.title: Solved example: end conditions
steps.body: Same rod fixed–free (K = 2): P_cr = 15.5/4 = **3.9 kN**. Fixed–fixed (K = 0.5): P_cr = 15.5×4 = **62.0 kN**. End fixity matters more than material.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the larger I (strong axis) instead of the minimum I.
- Applying Euler to short columns (σ_cr above the proportional limit).
- Forgetting K for non-pinned ends.

activity.prompt: Pinned aluminium rod: d = 20 mm, L = 600 mm, E = 72,000 N/mm². Euler critical load (kN).

lessons.title: Lab: Johnson parabola and column design

scenes.text: Most real aircraft struts are intermediate in length: they neither crush nor follow Euler's curve.
Johnson's parabola bridges the two.

steps.title: Johnson–Euler
steps.body:
Transition slenderness (where the Euler curve meets σ_y/2): **λ_c = π√(2E/σ_y)**. For λ < λ_c use the **Johnson parabola**: **σ_cr = σ_y [1 − σ_y λ²/(4π²E)]**; for λ > λ_c use Euler (σ_cr = π²E/λ²). The parabola is tangent to Euler at λ_c and gives σ_cr = σ_y at λ = 0.

For aluminium alloys (E = 72 GPa, σ_y = 345 MPa): λ_c = π√(2×72,000/345) = **64.2**. Real design uses test-based column curves with a knockdown factor; wing struts also have end fixity factors.

steps.title: Solved example: required area
steps.body: Strut length 800 mm (pinned) must carry 30 kN (ultimate). Try a solid round rod d = 30 mm: r = 7.5 mm, λ = 800/7.5 = 106.7 > 64.2, so Euler applies: σ_cr = π²×72,000/106.7² = 62.5 MPa; capacity = 62.5×706.9 mm² = 44.1 kN > 30 kN → MS = 44.1/30 − 1 = 0.47. A hollow tube of the same area has a larger r and a higher σ_cr, so it is lighter.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using Euler below λ_c.
- Ignoring local buckling of thin-walled tubes (crippling).
- Forgetting end-fixity uncertainty: use K conservatively.

activity.prompt: 2024-T3 (E = 72 GPa, σ_y = 345 MPa), λ = 40: Johnson σ_cr = σ_y[1 − σ_yλ²/(4π²E)] (MPa).

lessons.title: Lab: Buckling of thin plates in compression and shear

scenes.text: The thin upper wing skin under compression ripples between stringers long before the panel fails.
Plate buckling theory predicts when.

steps.title: Plate buckling
steps.body:
For a rectangular plate (width b, thickness t, simply supported on all edges) under uniform compression:

**σ_cr = k_c π²E/(12(1 − ν²)) (t/b)²**, where **k_c = 4** for a long plate with simply supported edges (k_c = (m b/a + a/(m b))², minimum 4 at integer a/b); k_c ≈ 6.35 for clamped loaded-edge/ simply supported unloaded edges; for a plate with one free unloaded edge k_c = 0.425.
Shear: **τ_cr = k_s π²E/(12(1 − ν²)) (t/b)²**, with b the shorter side, k_s = 5.35 + 4(b/a)² (simply supported) → 5.35 for long plates.

Unlike a column, a plate has **post-buckling strength**: after buckling it carries more load via the stiff edges (effective width) — the basis of semi-monocoque design.

steps.title: Solved example: skin panel
steps.body:
b = 100 mm, t = 1.5 mm, E = 72 GPa, ν = 0.33: π²E/(12(1 − ν²)) = 9.8696×72,000/10.693 = 66,457 MPa. (t/b)² = 2.25×10⁻⁴. σ_cr = 4×66,457×2.25×10⁻⁴ = **59.8 MPa**.
Stress is only 17% of yield: the skin buckles long before the stringers yield.

steps.title: Solved example: web shear buckling
steps.body: Web panel b = 200 mm (short side), t = 1.0 mm, long: τ_cr = 5.35×66,457×(1/200)² = 5.35×66,457×2.5×10⁻⁵ = **8.9 MPa**. A web carrying q = 66.7 N/mm sees τ = 66.7 MPa ≫ 8.9: it will buckle in shear and must be designed as a tension-field web (next lesson) or stiffened.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the long side as b in shear.
- Taking buckling as failure of a plate in a stiffened structure.
- Using k = 4 for plates with free edges.

lessons.title: Lab: Effective width and tension-field webs

story.title: A web that buckles but still works

scenes.text: Aircraft spar webs are so thin that they buckle in shear at low load — and then carry load by diagonal tension like a cable net.
Wagner's tension-field theory (1929) turned this into a design method.

steps.title: Effective width (von Kármán)
steps.body:
After buckling, load concentrates near the stiffened edges. A buckled plate carries the same load as an unbuckled strip of **effective width b_e = π t √(E/(3(1 − ν²)σ_e)) ≈ 1.9 t √(E/σ_e)** at edge stress σ_e (maximum b_e = b). Panel strength = σ_e (A_stiffener + b_e t).

**Pure diagonal tension (Wagner)**: the web, buckled in shear, carries the shear by tension along the diagonal at angle α ≈ 45°. For α = 45° and a web of height h carrying shear S: shear flow q = S/h; diagonal tension stress **σ_t = 2q/t = 2S/(h t)** (for α = 45°; in general σ_t = q/(t sinα cosα)). The flanges then carry additional bending from the tension field, and the vertical stiffeners are loaded in compression.

steps.title: Solved example: effective width
steps.body: t = 1.5 mm, E = 72,000 MPa, edge stress σ_e = 200 MPa: b_e = 1.9×1.5×√(72,000/200) = 2.85×18.97 = **54.1 mm** (if b = 100 mm the skin is effective over 54%).

steps.title: Solved example: tension-field web
steps.body: S = 20 kN, h = 300 mm, t = 1.0 mm: q = 66.7 N/mm. Pure tension field at 45°: σ_t = 2×66.7/1.0 = **133 MPa** (below 2024-T3's yield of 345); the shear-buckling stress was 8.9 MPa: the web is heavily buckled but safe provided the flanges and stiffeners can resist the load (the vertical stiffeners must be checked for the resulting compression).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the web in pure shear when it is in the tension-field regime.
- Forgetting the effective width of the *stiffener flange*.
- Overlooking rivet/bolt loads, which become very high in diagonal tension.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – Compression strength of a skin–stringer panel

scenes.text: The upper wing panel is a thin skin riveted to stringers: it buckles locally, but the stringers keep carrying.
You find the load at which the stringer reaches its crippling stress.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
1. Stringer failure stress σ_f (crippling or yield).
2. Effective width of skin at σ_f: b_e = 1.9 t √(E/σ_f) (≤ b).
3. Load per bay: **P = σ_f (A_stringer + b_e t)**.
4. Compare with the average stress over the full bay area.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Pitch b = 100 mm, skin t = 1.5 mm, stringer A_s = 120 mm², E = 72,000 MPa, σ_f = 280 MPa.
b_e = 1.9×1.5×√(72,000/280) = 2.85×16.04 = **45.7 mm**; skin area effective = 68.6 mm².
P = 280×(120 + 68.6) = **52.8 kN per bay**.
Full area = 120 + 150 = 270 mm² → average stress σ_avg = 52,800/270 = **195.5 MPa** (70% of σ_f).

steps.title: Solved example: bending effect
steps.body: For a wing with 12 such bays across the upper surface in compression, N = 12×52.8 = 634 kN: the maximum bending moment over a box depth h = 400 mm (taking the lower surface as the tension flange) is M ≈ N×h = 634×0.4 = 253 kN·m.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the whole skin width when it is buckled.
- Taking σ_f as yield when crippling governs.
- Ignoring inter-rivet buckling and column buckling of stringer + skin between ribs.

lessons.title: Lab: Fatigue – S–N curves, Goodman and Miner's rule

scenes.text: In 1954 two de Havilland Comet airliners broke up in flight; investigators traced fatigue cracks at square window corners in the pressurised fuselage.
Since then fatigue life and damage tolerance have been central to aircraft structural certification.

steps.title: Fatigue basics
steps.body:
Cyclic stress (amplitude σ_a, mean σ_m, range Δσ = 2σ_a, ratio R = σ_min/σ_max) can cause failure well below σ_y after N cycles. **S–N (Wöhler) curves** plot stress vs cycles to failure; steels show an endurance limit (~0.5σ_u); aluminium has none: use the strength at 10⁷–10⁸ cycles. Stress concentration: **σ_max = K_t σ_nom** (hole in a wide plate K_t ≈ 3); notch sensitivity reduces the effective K_f.

**Mean-stress correction (Goodman)**: σ_a/σ_e + σ_m/σ_u = 1.
**Miner's linear damage rule**: **D = Σ n_i/N_i**; failure when D ≈ 1 (in practice 0.3–1; use scatter factors of 3–5).

steps.title: Solved example: Goodman
steps.body: σ_e = 150 MPa (fully reversed), σ_u = 480 MPa, σ_m = 100 MPa: allowable σ_a = 150×(1 − 100/480) = **118.8 MPa**.

steps.title: Solved example: Miner
steps.body: Block spectrum per 1,000 flights: n₁ = 2×10⁵ cycles at stress level 1 (N₁ = 10⁶); n₂ = 5×10⁴ at level 2 (N₂ = 2×10⁵); n₃ = 10⁴ at level 3 (N₃ = 5×10⁴). D = 0.20 + 0.25 + 0.20 = **0.65** per block, so about 1/0.65 = 1.54 blocks until D = 1 → life ≈ 1,540 flights (before scatter factor; with factor 4: 385 flights).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using ultimate strength for cyclic design.
- Ignoring K_t at holes, fillets and window corners (rounded corners are essential).
- Applying Miner without a scatter/safety factor.

lessons.title: Lab: Fracture mechanics – stress intensity and critical crack length

story.title: How big can a crack get?

scenes.text: An inspector finds a crack at a rivet hole; the engineer must tell whether it can cause fast fracture.
Linear elastic fracture mechanics gives the answer.

steps.title: LEFM
steps.body:
The stress field at a crack tip is characterised by the **stress intensity factor K = Y σ √(π a)** (MPa√m), Y a geometry factor (central crack in a wide plate: Y = 1; edge crack: Y ≈ 1.12). Fracture occurs when **K = K_c**; for thick sections (plane strain) K = K_IC, the fracture toughness. Typical values (plane strain, MPa√m, rounded): 2024-T351 ≈ 37, 7075-T651 ≈ 29, Ti-6Al-4V ≈ 55–75, high-strength steels 50–100. Thin sheet (plane stress) toughness is higher.

**Critical crack length**: **a_c = (1/π)(K_IC/(Yσ))²**; **critical stress** for a crack a: σ_c = K_IC/(Y√(πa)). Damage tolerance requires that cracks be found and repaired before reaching a_c.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
2024-T351: K_IC = 37 MPa√m; edge crack Y = 1.12; σ = 150 MPa: Yσ = 168 MPa. a_c = (1/π)(37/168)² = (1/π)(0.04851) = 0.01544 m = **15.4 mm**.
If σ is raised to 250 MPa: a_c = (1/π)(37/280)² = 5.6 mm: higher stress reduces critical crack size by (150/250)² = 0.36.

steps.title: Solved example: critical stress
steps.body: A 4 mm edge crack in 2024-T351: σ_c = 37/(1.12×√(π×0.004)) = 37/(1.12×0.1121) = **294.7 MPa**. Compare with the operating stress to find the residual strength factor.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing mm and m in √(πa).
- Using K_IC (plane strain) for thin sheet or K_c (plane stress) incorrectly.
- Assuming small cracks are harmless: they grow under fatigue.

activity.prompt: 2024-T351: K_IC = 37 MPa√m, Y = 1.12, σ = 150 MPa. Critical crack length a_c (mm).

quiz.q: Higher stress gives critical crack length

lessons.title: Lab: Paris-law crack growth and inspection interval

story.title: How long until the crack is dangerous?

scenes.text: A 2 mm crack is found at a lug hole. Management wants to know how many flights remain before it becomes critical.
Paris-law integration gives the number of cycles.

steps.title: Paris law
steps.body:
In the stable growth regime: **da/dN = C (ΔK)^m**, ΔK = Y Δσ √(πa). Integrate from initial a_i to final a_f (constant Y, Δσ):

**N = [a_i^{1−m/2} − a_f^{1−m/2}] / [(m/2 − 1) C (YΔσ)^m π^{m/2}]** (m ≠ 2).

In damage-tolerance practice, the inspection interval is a fraction (e.g. half) of the calculated life from the detectable crack size to a_c, so that at least two inspections occur before failure ('fail-safe' and 'safe-life' are other philosophies).

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Assume C = 10⁻¹¹ (m/cycle, MPa√m), m = 3, Y = 1.12, Δσ = 100 MPa, a_i = 2 mm, a_f = a_c = 15.4 mm (from the previous lesson).
a_i^{−0.5} = 1/√0.002 = 22.36; a_f^{−0.5} = 8.058; difference = 14.30.
(YΔσ)³ = 112³ = 1.405×10⁶; π^{1.5} = 5.568. Denominator = 0.5×10⁻¹¹×1.405×10⁶×5.568 = 3.912×10⁻⁵.
**N = 14.30/3.912×10⁻⁵ = 3.66×10⁵ cycles**. With one cycle per flight, 366,000 flights; the inspection interval = N/2 = 183,000 flights (illustrative data).

steps.title: Solved example: sensitivity
steps.body: Because N ∝ (Δσ)^−m with m = 3, a 20% increase in stress range cuts the life to 1/1.2³ = **58%**. This is why overloads, corrosion pits and rework matter.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using a_f larger than the critical crack length.
- Forgetting that C and m are material/environment dependent: use tested data.
- Ignoring crack retardation after overloads and acceleration in corrosion.

lessons.title: Lab: Composite laminae – rule of mixtures and ply stresses

scenes.text: Modern airliners carry about half their structural weight in carbon-fibre composites.
Fibres give strength and stiffness along their direction; the matrix holds them together.

steps.title: Micromechanics
steps.body:
For a unidirectional lamina with fibre volume fraction V_f (V_m = 1 − V_f):
- **E₁ = V_f E_f + V_m E_m** (rule of mixtures, along fibres)
- **1/E₂ = V_f/E_f + V_m/E_m** (inverse rule, transverse; approximate/lower bound)
- **ν₁₂ = V_f ν_f + V_m ν_m**; **ρ = V_f ρ_f + V_m ρ_m**.

Ply stress transformation (θ = angle between fibres and load axis x): σ₁ = σ_x cos²θ + σ_y sin²θ + 2τ_xy sinθ cosθ; σ₂ = σ_x sin²θ + σ_y cos²θ − 2τ_xy sinθ cosθ; τ₁₂ = (σ_y − σ_x) sinθ cosθ + τ_xy(cos²θ − sin²θ). Failure criteria: max stress, max strain, **Tsai–Hill**, **Tsai–Wu**. Laminates are described by the ABD matrix; common layups are quasi-isotropic [0/±45/90]_s. Composites are strong in tension along fibres but weak in transverse tension, interlaminar shear and impact (barely-visible impact damage is a design driver).

steps.title: Solved example: off-axis ply
steps.body: A ply at θ = 30° loaded σ_x = 100 MPa (σ_y = τ_xy = 0): σ₁ = 100 cos²30° = **75 MPa**; σ₂ = 100 sin²30° = **25 MPa**; τ₁₂ = −100 sin30° cos30° = **−43.3 MPa**. The transverse and shear stresses (25, 43) are close to the weak lamina allowables, which is why ±45° plies are used sparingly.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating a composite as isotropic.
- Forgetting that the rule of mixtures for E₂ is only a rough estimate (Halpin–Tsai/Chamis are better).
- Ignoring moisture, temperature and impact knockdowns.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – A cracked lower-wing skin: inspect, assess, decide

story.title: Finding at 06:30 during a heavy check

scenes.text: An inspector finds a 4 mm crack radiating from a fastener hole in the lower wing skin of a regional turboprop.
The aircraft is due to fly in three hours. Safety, schedule and structures all collide.

steps.title: Structural layout and damage tolerance
steps.body:
**Semi-monocoque structure**: skin carries shear and part of bending; stringers/longerons carry axial load; ribs/frames maintain shape and introduce loads; spars carry wing bending and shear. Wing box: upper skin in compression (buckling-critical), lower skin in tension (fatigue-critical, damage tolerance-critical). Fuselage: skin carries hoop stress from pressure; frames and stringers stiffen it; crack-stoppers (tear straps) arrest cracks. **Fail-safe** = multiple load paths; **damage tolerance** = crack growth analysis and inspections.

In practice an engineer follows the aircraft's structural repair manual (SRM) and escalates to the design authority: quick calculations support, not replace, the approved procedure.

steps.title: Quick numbers
steps.body: K_IC = 37 MPa√m, Y = 1.12, a = 4 mm: critical stress = 294.7 MPa. Operating limit stress in the lower skin ≈ 150 MPa: residual strength factor = 294.7/150 = 1.96 — the structure can still carry limit load, but fatigue growth must be assessed (Paris law).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating a calculated residual strength as permission to defer repair.
- Releasing an aircraft on an unapproved repair.
- Giving engineering incomplete inspection data.

a.text: A 4 mm crack is found at a fastener hole in the lower wing skin before the morning departure. What do you do first?

choices.label: Record the finding, ground the aircraft, and notify the structures engineer and quality
choices.feedback: Correct: a safety-critical finding is documented and escalated; the aircraft is not released until an approved disposition exists.

choices.label: Seal it with sealant and release the aircraft: the crack is small
choices.feedback: Sealant does not restore strength; releasing a cracked primary structure without approved repair is unsafe and non-compliant.

choices.label: Drill a small hole at the crack tip yourself and fly
choices.feedback: Stop-drilling is a repair only if the repair manual or engineering approval allows it; it is not a field improvisation.

b.text: The engineer asks you for the data needed to assess the crack. What do you supply?

choices.label: Crack length and orientation, hole location, material and thickness, photos, NDT results (eddy current), and flight cycles/hours
choices.feedback: Right: these inputs allow a damage-tolerance assessment.

choices.label: Only 'there is a crack'
choices.feedback: Insufficient: the assessment needs size, location and loading history.

c.text: Engineering calculates a residual strength factor of 1.96 and a remaining life of a few thousand flights, but the manual requires a repair at this crack size. What is the correct disposition?

choices.label: Perform the approved repair (e.g. cold-working/oversize hole with a new fastener or a doubler per the SRM), then re-inspect and update the records
choices.feedback: Correct: the approved repair restores the damage-tolerance basis, followed by inspection and documentation.

choices.label: Defer the repair for six months because the residual strength is high
choices.feedback: Residual strength alone is not sufficient: the crack grows with every flight and the approved disposition is mandatory.

x1.text: The aircraft flies cracked. A regulator audit later finds the missing repair. Rework: restart from the correct first step.

x2.text: Unapproved modification. The aircraft is grounded by quality, and a report is raised. Rework from the start.

x3.text: Engineering cannot assess without data and requests a re-inspection: schedule delay. Provide complete data next time.

x4.text: The crack grows and the next inspection finds it at 9 mm; the aircraft is grounded for a major repair. Always follow the approved disposition.

end1.text: The aircraft is repaired, inspected and released with full records. Structural integrity and safety are preserved.

lessons.title: Formula and key-point sheet

scenes.text: A stress-engineering interview or exam often reduces to a dozen equations.
Knowing when each applies matters more than the algebra.

steps.title: Stress, strain, failure and loads
steps.body:
- σ = P/A; ε = ΔL/L; σ = Eε; G = E/(2(1+ν)).
- Mohr: σ₁,₂ = (σx + σy)/2 ± √(((σx − σy)/2)² + τ²); tan2θ_p = 2τ/(σx − σy).
- von Mises (plane): √(σ₁² − σ₁σ₂ + σ₂²) = σ_y; Tresca: σ₁ − σ₃ = σ_y.
- Thin cylinder: σ_h = pr/t; σ_L = pr/2t.
- Load factor n = L/W; turn n = 1/cosφ; V_A = V_s√n; ultimate = 1.5 × limit; MS = allowable/applied − 1.

steps.title: Beams, shear flow, torsion
steps.body:
- σ = M y/I; 1/R = M/EI; cantilever P: PL³/3EI; UDL: wL⁴/8EI; SS centre load: PL³/48EI; SS UDL: 5wL⁴/384EI.
- Shear flow q = −(S/I)∫t y ds; τ = q/t; boom method Δq = −S B y/I; channel e = 3b²/(h+6b).
- Closed section: q = T/2A; dθ/dz = (q/2AG)∮ds/t; J = 4A²/∮ds/t.
- Open section: J = Σbt³/3; τ = T t/J.
- Multicell: T = Σ2A_iq_i with equal twist.

steps.title: Energy, buckling, fatigue, fracture
steps.body:
- U = ∫M²/2EI dx; δ = ∂U/∂P; truss δ = ΣFfL/AE; propped cantilever R = 3wL/8.

steps.title: Top mistakes
steps.body:
- Using limit instead of ultimate loads with ultimate allowables.
- Using J = Σbt³/3 on a closed section.
- Forgetting minimum I in Euler.
- Mixing N, mm and MPa with N/m².

lessons.title: Lab: Tensile test of an aluminium specimen

scenes.text: A universal testing machine pulls a standard round aluminium specimen at a constant crosshead speed.
Load and extensometer readings give the stress–strain curve.

steps.title: Aim, apparatus, procedure
steps.body:
**Aim**: determine E, 0.2% proof stress, ultimate tensile strength, elongation and reduction of area.
**Apparatus**: UTM, extensometer (gauge length L₀ = 50 mm), vernier/micrometer, aluminium alloy specimen d₀ = 10 mm.
**Procedure**: measure d₀ and mark L₀; mount specimen in the grips; attach the extensometer; apply load at a constant slow rate; record load–extension to fracture; fit the broken halves and measure L_f and d_f.

steps.title: Sources of error
steps.body: Grip slip, misaligned specimen, extensometer calibration, strain-rate effects, measuring the cross-section after necking incorrectly (use initial area for engineering stress).

lessons.title: Lab: Cantilever deflection and Maxwell's reciprocal theorem

scenes.text: A 25 × 3 mm aluminium strip is clamped as a cantilever; dial gauges measure deflection at two points.
Loading point A and measuring at B, then loading B and measuring at A, gives the same deflection.

steps.title: Aim and theory
steps.body:
**Aim**: determine E from tip deflection and verify Maxwell's reciprocal theorem δ_AB = δ_BA.
**Theory**: δ = PL³/(3EI) at the tip; for a load at distance a and deflection at x < a: δ(x) = P x²(3a − x)/(6EI). I = bh³/12.
**Procedure**: clamp the strip, hang weights from hangers at A (L = 300 mm) and B (200 mm), record the dial readings, repeat loading B and reading A; plot δ vs P.

steps.title: Observations
steps.body:
b = 25 mm, h = 3 mm → I = 25×27/12 = 56.25 mm⁴; L = 300 mm.
| P (N) | δ_tip (mm) |
|---|---|
| 1 | 2.30 |
| 2 | 4.60 |
| 3 | 6.88 |

E = PL³/(3Iδ) = 2×2.7×10⁷/(3×56.25×4.60) = **69.6 GPa** (theory for Al: ≈ 70 GPa).
Maxwell test: P = 2 N at A, reading at B = 1.52 mm; P = 2 N at B, reading at A = 1.50 mm → equal within 1.3% (dial resolution).

steps.title: Sources of error
steps.body: Clamp compliance, dial-gauge friction, strip thickness variation (δ ∝ 1/h³: a 2% error in h gives 6% in I), self-weight.

lessons.title: Lab: Buckling of a slender strut (Euler) with viva questions

scenes.text: A thin steel strip, 20 × 2 mm, 400 mm long, is loaded between knife edges.
The examiner asks why it bends sideways about the weaker axis.

steps.title: Aim and theory
steps.body:
**Aim**: verify P_cr = π²EI/L_e² for pinned ends and plot a Southwell plot to estimate P_cr from pre-buckling readings.
**Theory**: I_min = bh³/12 = 20×8/12 = 13.33 mm⁴; E = 200 GPa; L = 400 mm → P_cr = π²×200,000×13.33/160,000 = **164.5 N**. **Southwell plot**: δ/P vs δ is a straight line of slope 1/P_cr.

steps.title: Observations
steps.body:
| P (N) | lateral δ (mm) | δ/P (mm/N) |
|---|---|---|
| 40 | 0.30 | 0.0075 |
| 75 | 0.78 | 0.0104 |
| 108 | 1.80 | 0.0167 |
| 128 | 3.30 | 0.0258 |

The slope of the δ/P vs δ line: (0.0258 − 0.0075)/(3.30 − 0.30) = 0.0061 per N → **P_cr ≈ 1/0.0061 = 164 N**, in agreement with the theoretical 164.5 N; the intercept (0.0057 mm/N) is the initial out-of-straightness effect.

steps.title: Sources of error
steps.body: Initial curvature, end friction on knife edges, load eccentricity, plastic yield if overloaded.

activity.prompt: Typical viva questions with model answers.

items.q: Why does the strip buckle about the weaker axis?
items.a: Because I_min is smaller; P_cr ∝ I and the strut bends in the direction of least resistance.

items.q: What changes if the ends are fixed instead of pinned?
items.a: The effective length halves (K = 0.5) and P_cr rises four times.

items.q: Why do real columns fail below the Euler load?
items.a: Initial imperfections, eccentric loading and residual stresses cause bending from the start; and short columns yield before buckling.

items.q: What is the slenderness ratio?
items.a: λ = L_e/r with r = √(I/A); Euler applies for large λ.

items.q: What is a Southwell plot?
items.a: A plot of δ/P against δ whose slope is 1/P_cr; it predicts P_cr without loading to failure.

items.q: How is buckling different from yielding?
items.a: Buckling is a stability loss that depends on stiffness (E, I, L); yielding depends on strength (σ_y).

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – Previous-year-style problem set

scenes.text: The paper has four structures problems: stress, buckling, shear flow and a thin-walled cylinder.
Sketch first, state assumptions, then compute.

steps.title: Problem 1 – plane stress (original)
steps.body:
σx = 60, σy = −20, τxy = 40 MPa. Find the principal stresses and principal angle.
**Solution**: C = 20; R = √(40² + 40²) = 56.57. σ₁ = **76.6 MPa**, σ₂ = **−36.6 MPa**; tan2θ_p = 80/80 = 1 → θ_p = **22.5°**.

steps.title: Problem 2 – column (original)
steps.body:
A pinned tube, OD 40 mm, ID 36 mm, L = 1.5 m, E = 70 GPa. Find P_cr and check Euler's validity.
**Solution**: I = π(40⁴ − 36⁴)/64 = 43,215 mm⁴; A = 238.8 mm²; r = 13.45 mm; λ = 111.5. P_cr = π²×70,000×43,215/1500² = **13.3 kN**; σ_cr = 55.6 MPa ≪ σ_y → Euler valid.

steps.title: Problem 3 – pressurised fuselage (original)
steps.body:
r = 1.5 m, t = 1.2 mm, Δp = 50 kPa. Find hoop and longitudinal stresses and the von Mises stress.
**Solution**: σ_h = 50,000×1.5/0.0012 = **62.5 MPa**; σ_L = **31.25 MPa**; σ_vm = √(62.5² − 62.5×31.25 + 31.25²) = √2930 = **54.1 MPa**.

steps.title: Problem 4 – torsion of a box (original)
steps.body:
A single-cell box with mid-line area 45,000 mm², wall t = 1.2 mm, carries T = 3 kN·m. Find q and τ.
**Solution**: q = 3×10⁶/(2×45,000) = **33.3 N/mm**; τ = 33.3/1.2 = **27.8 MPa**.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Check units (N, mm, MPa), draw the free-body diagram, and test the answer against a limiting case.
